===FILE:apps/flagship-foundry/docs/adr/adr-010-rollout-rollback-and-incident-documentation-model.md===# ADR-010: Define Rollout, Rollback, and Incident Documentation Model ## Status accepted ## Date 2026-03-23 ## Context `WO-FF-010` is the final `M4` work order for go/no-go and operating-model closure. The initiative already has structured artifacts for plans, approvals, runs, evidence, runbooks, personas, and continuity, but it does not yet have one documented model for how rollout, rollback, and incident records relate to each other. Relevant existing building blocks include: - runbook contracts in `flagship-foundry-work/schemas/runbook.schema.json` - run and execution history contracts in `flagship-foundry-work/schemas/run.schema.json` and `flagship-foundry-work/schemas/run-timeline.schema.json` - continuity contract authority in `flagship-foundry-work/schemas/continuity-state.schema.json` - operational runbooks under `flagship-foundry-work/runbooks/` - approval state under `flagship-foundry-work/state/approvals/` - plan state under `flagship-foundry-work/state/plans/` - run state under `flagship-foundry-work/state/runs/` The gap is not whether documentation exists, but whether the operational narrative is consistently modeled. `M4` needs a clear rule for which artifacts constitute rollout records, rollback records, and incident records, and how they tie back to approvals, evidence, and continuity state. ## Options Considered ### Option A: Use free-form markdown or chat notes for operations **Description**: Let operators document rollout, rollback, and incidents in whatever format is convenient. **Pros**: Flexible and low-friction. **Cons**: Inconsistent handoff quality, poor machine-readability, and weak continuity for later agents. ### Option B: Use one generic release checklist for everything **Description**: Collapse rollout, rollback, and incidents into a single checklist artifact. **Pros**: Simpler than multiple artifact types. **Cons**: Blurs different operational scenarios and weakens incident-specific learning. ### Option C: Use a structured runbook-backed documentation model linked to state and evidence **Description**: Model rollout, rollback, and incidents as related but distinct documentation flows anchored in runbooks, approvals, runs, and continuity. **Pros**: Supports deterministic handoff, machine-readable traceability, and better operational learning. **Cons**: Requires more discipline than free-form notes. ## Decision Choose **Option C**. Documentation model: - Rollout, rollback, and incident handling must be modeled as structured operational records, not only narrative prose. - The canonical process shape comes from runbook contracts and existing runbook assets, especially the delivery and telemetry-oriented runbooks. - State artifacts remain the source data for what happened; operator-facing documentation must link back to them rather than restating them manually. Minimum linkage requirements: - Every rollout record must identify the governing plan, approval artifact, run or runs executed, and supporting evidence bundle. - Every rollback record must identify the trigger, the boundary being rolled back, the stopping point, and the retained evidence for diagnosis. - Every incident record must identify the triggering signal, impacted system, verifier evidence, and any resulting fix-memory or guardrail update proposal. - Operational closeout must update continuity pointers so the next agent or operator knows the next command set and open risks. Milestone alignment: - `WO-FF-010` closes only when `M4` has a documented go/no-go model that references actual plan, approval, run, and evidence artifacts. - `M3` adapter and telemetry evidence becomes an input to the incident and rollback record, not a disconnected appendix. - The documentation model must support both release-style rollout and incident-driven rollback without requiring a separate one-off process. ## Consequences ### Positive - Gives Foundry a reusable operating model instead of milestone-specific ceremony. - Improves resumability because operational docs point back to canonical state and continuity artifacts. - Connects incidents to learning loops through fix-memory and guardrail updates. ### Negative - Operators must maintain structured records even when a free-form note would feel faster. - Some existing runbooks may need refinement so the model is consistently applied. ### Risks - If operator-facing documents duplicate too much state, they may drift from the canonical artifacts they are supposed to summarize. - If continuity updates are skipped, the documentation model may still fail resumability even with good incident notes. - If incident records do not link to evidence and learning outputs, the model may become procedural rather than improving system quality. ## References - ===FILE:apps/flagship-foundry/docs/adr/adr-011-foundry-directory-layout-and-continuity-instance.md===# ADR-011: `.foundry` Directory Layout and Continuity Instance Location ## Status accepted ## Date 2026-03-23 ## Context ADR-002 established **Option C**: the continuity **contract** lives in `flagship-foundry-work/schemas/continuity-state.schema.json`, while the **runtime instance** was pinned to **`.codex/projects/<project>/current-task.json`**. Operators and multi-agent workflows need a **vendor-neutral** root for Foundry-owned continuity so project state is not implied to be **Codex-specific**. The schema currently **restricts** `authority.runtimeInstanceAuthority` to a `.codex/...` pattern, which blocks moving the instance without a contract change. Forces: - **ADR-002** split (contract vs instance) must remain; only the **instance path** and **on-disk layout** change. - **Simplicity**: avoid deep trees under `.foundry/` until there is a concrete consumer (per ontology discipline). - **Migration**: existing repos may already have `.codex/projects/**`; need a clear story without silent data loss (**ADR-004** alignment for projections/overwrites). - **Import pipeline** (`import-pipeline.mjs`) treats `.codex/` as high-signal workspace content; Foundry metadata under `.foundry/` should be **discoverable** without conflating with Codex app config. ## Options Considered ### Option A: Single file at repo root (`.foundry/current-task.json`) **Description**: One continuity file for the whole repository. **Pros**: Minimal path depth; trivial to document. **Cons**: Does not scale to **multiple Foundry projects** in one monorepo; conflicts with `init-project <name>` today, which is **per project name**. ### Option B: Flat `.foundry/<slug>/` without a `projects/` segment **Description**: Paths like `.foundry/my-app/current-task.json`. **Pros**: Shorter paths. **Cons**: Mixes “registry of projects” with future top-level folders (templates, cache); harder to reserve **namespaces** for non-project artifacts. ### Option C: Namespace layout — `.foundry/projects/<slug>/` as canonical (recommended) **Description**: - **Canonical continuity instance**: `.foundry/projects/<projectSlug>/current-task.json` - **Charter** (same as today): `.foundry/projects/<projectSlug>/SDLC_CHARTER.md` - **Schema pattern** for `authority.runtimeInstanceAuthority`: `^\.foundry/projects/[^/]+/current-task\.json$` - **Optional** (human-only, not validated by continuity schema in v1): `.foundry/README.md` explaining the folder—operators may commit or gitignore it. - **Explicitly out of scope for v1** (reserved names; do not create by default): `.foundry/cache/`, `.foundry/templates/` — add only when a feature needs them. **Pros**: Aligns with existing **per-project** continuity semantics; clear separation between **project instances** and future **shared** folders; matches intent packet diagrams; keeps blast radius of migrations bounded to `projects/`. **Cons**: Slightly longer paths; requires one-time migration from `.codex/projects/`. ## Decision Choose **Option C**. - The **runtime instance authority** for Flagship Foundry continuity is **`.foundry/projects/<project>/current-task.json`** (repo-relative POSIX path string in JSON). - **ADR-002 Option C** remains in force: **contract authority** stays the Foundry schema; **instance authority** is updated from `.codex/...` to `.foundry/...` as defined here. - **Legacy `.codex/projects/`** may remain on disk for **other tools**; Foundry runtime reads/writes **`.foundry/projects/`** after implementation. **Migration** is documented separately (copy, symlink, or dual-write during transition)—not part of this ADR’s normative layout. - **`derivedMirrors`** in `current-task.json` may list former `.codex/projects/.../current-task.json` paths during migration for audit only; mirrors are **non-authoritative** per ADR-002. ## Consequences ### Positive - Continuity location is **branded and agent-agnostic**. - Clear place for **multiple projects** in one repo. - Room for future **non-project** subtrees under `.foundry/` without colliding with project slugs. ### Negative - Requires coordinated updates: **schema pattern**, **`continuity.mjs`**, **tests**, **cursor rules** referencing `.codex/projects/**/current-task.json`, and any **bootstrap** docs. - Teams must run a **one-time migration** or accept parallel folders during cutover. ### Risks - Stale automation referencing `.codex` for Foundry continuity causes **split-brain** if not updated in one pass. - Accidental commit of **secrets** into `.foundry/` — mitigate with `.gitignore` guidance for local-only files (charters and task JSON should be reviewable; env secrets should not appear). ## References - `flagship-foundry-work/docs/adr/adr-002-continuity-schema-authority-and-bootstrap.md` - `flagship-foundry-work/schemas/continuity-state.schema.json` - `flagship-foundry-work/packages/core/src/continuity.mjs` - `flagship-foundry-work/docs/intent/intent-foundry-dot-foundry-ecosystem-init-2026-03-23.md`
===FILE:apps/flagship-foundry/docs/adr/adr-011a-foundry-ssot-personas-skills-layout.md===# ADR-011a: `.foundry` SSOT Layout for Personas, Skills, and Agent Definitions ## Status proposed ## Date 2026-03-23 ## Context ADR-011 established `.foundry/projects/<slug>/` as the canonical location for per-project continuity instances (`current-task.json`, `SDLC_CHARTER.md`). That ADR explicitly reserved future non-project subtrees under `.foundry/` but deferred decisions on three categories of Foundry-owned content: 1. **Personas** (13 structured JSON files currently in `flagship-foundry-work/personas/`): agent personality packs that define role, purpose, activation criteria, and guardrail/runbook bindings. 2. **Skills** (10 procedural markdown documents currently duplicated in `.cursor/skills/` and `.claude/skills/`): executable step-by-step procedures invoked by agents. 3. **Agent definitions** (8 markdown files currently duplicated in `.cursor/agents/` and `.claude/agents/`): role descriptions, phase bindings, forbidden behaviors, and output contracts for specialist agents. Today, these three artifact types are fragmented: - Personas live only in `flagship-foundry-work/personas/` and are not discoverable under `.foundry/`. - Skills are fully duplicated across `.cursor/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. The bodies are nearly identical; differences are limited to path references (e.g., `flagship-foundry/` vs `foundry/flagship-foundry-work/`) and frontmatter fields specific to each tool (Cursor uses `model:` for routing; Claude Code uses `effort:`). - Agent definitions are duplicated across `.cursor/agents/<name>.md` and `.claude/agents/<name>.md`. The `.claude/` versions are consistently more detailed (fuller quality gate descriptions, more skills listed, architectural principles enumerated). The `.cursor/` versions are condensed and route to different model identifiers (`composer-2-fast`, `gpt-5.4-medium`). This duplication violates the **artifact-authority** principle: there is no single canonical text for Foundry-owned behavioral content. Drift has already occurred in path references across the two environments. Three open questions require resolution before implementation (wo-003) can proceed: 1. Should personas live at `.foundry/personas/` (flat, repo-wide) or `.foundry/projects/<slug>/personas/` (per-project scoped)? 2. Should skills use `.foundry/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (directory-per-skill mirroring existing structure) or a manifest-generated stub approach? 3. What is the dual-read window duration and logging strategy for the `.codex/` fallback path? ## Options Considered ### Question 1: Persona Subpath #### Option 1A: Flat repo-wide — `.foundry/personas/<id>.json` **Description**: All 13 persona JSON files live directly under `.foundry/personas/`. The `$schema` ref updates to point to the Foundry schema location. No project-slug segmentation. **Pros**: - Personas are inherently cross-cutting: `persona:ecosystem-orchestrator` and `persona:independent-verifier` apply to any project in the monorepo. - Matches the existing flat structure under `flagship-foundry-work/personas/`. - Simpler discovery contract: glob `.foundry/personas/*.json`, validate against `persona-pack.schema.json`. - Avoids premature nesting per ADR-011's ontology discipline ("avoid deep trees until there is a concrete consumer"). **Cons**: - If a future project needs a project-scoped persona override, there is no namespace for it at this level. - All personas are visible to all projects, which may be noise for single-project use. #### Option 1B: Per-project scoped — `.foundry/projects/<slug>/personas/<id>.json` **Description**: Personas are nested under each project's directory. **Pros**: - Supports project-specific persona sets. - Keeps all project-related configuration in one tree. **Cons**: - Requires duplicating persona files across projects in a monorepo, contradicting SSOT. - All 13 current personas are repo-wide (none reference a specific project slug). - Creates deep nesting: `.foundry/projects/flagship-foundry/personas/ecosystem-orchestrator.json` is unwieldy. - No current consumer needs project-scoped personas. ### Question 2: Skills Format #### Option 2A: Directory-per-skill — `.foundry/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` **Description**: Mirror the existing `.cursor/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` directory structure. Each skill is a directory containing at minimum a `SKILL.md` file; additional assets (templates, examples) may be co-located. **Pros**: - Familiar structure; both Cursor and Claude Code already use this layout. - Allows co-location of auxiliary files per skill (e.g., a template or schema used by the skill). - No tooling changes needed to the skill loading path beyond updating the base directory. - Human-readable; discoverable with `ls .foundry/skills/`. **Cons**: - 10 directories is modestly verbose at the filesystem level. - Environment-specific frontmatter (model routing, tool-specific keys) must be handled by the overlay, not the base file. #### Option 2B: Manifest-generated stubs **Description**: A single `.foundry/skills/manifest.json` defines skill metadata. At build or init time, a generator produces stub files in `.cursor/skills/` and `.claude/skills/` from the manifest plus the canonical SKILL.md body. **Pros**: - Single manifest as the registry; enforces consistency by construction. - Environment-specific frontmatter is templated from the manifest. **Cons**: - Requires implementing and maintaining a generator tool. - Generated files are harder to review in git diffs (are they stale? regenerated?). - Adds a build step dependency; skill content is not immediately readable without running the generator. - No existing consumer for this manifest pattern; premature tooling per ontology discipline. ### Question 3: Dual-Read Window #### Option 3A: 30-day dual-read with structured logging **Description**: After `.foundry/` paths are canonical, `continuity.mjs` and the import pipeline try `.foundry/projects/<slug>/current-task.json` first. On miss, fall back to `.codex/projects/<slug>/current-task.json` with a `WARN`-level log message including the legacy path. After 30 calendar days from the merge date of the migration commit, the fallback path is removed in a follow-up commit. **Pros**: - Bounded window prevents indefinite technical debt. - 30 days covers typical sprint and release cycles. - Structured logging makes fallback usage observable and auditable. **Cons**: - Requires a follow-up cleanup commit (low cost). - 30 days may be too long for a fast-moving team or too short for teams with slower release cadences. #### Option 3B: No dual-read; hard cutover with symlinks **Description**: Create symlinks from `.codex/projects/<slug>/current-task.json` to `.foundry/projects/<slug>/current-task.json`. No code-level fallback. **Pros**: - Simplest code path; no conditional reads. **Cons**: - Symlinks have cross-platform issues (Windows Git default does not follow symlinks). - If a tool resolves symlinks differently, it may write to the wrong location. - No observability of which path was accessed. ## Decision ### Question 1: Personas at `.foundry/personas/<id>.json` (flat, repo-wide) — Option 1A Personas are cross-cutting by nature. All 13 existing personas define Foundry-wide agent roles (ecosystem-orchestrator, independent-verifier, chrome-extension-mv3-sme, etc.) with no project-specific binding. Nesting them under `projects/<slug>/` would either require duplication across projects (violating SSOT) or an arbitrary choice of which project "owns" them. The flat layout is simpler, matches the existing structure, and follows ADR-011's guidance to avoid deep trees until a concrete consumer demands them. If project-scoped persona overrides are needed in the future, the convention `.foundry/projects/<slug>/persona-overrides/<id>.json` can be introduced as an additive extension without breaking the base layout. ### Question 2: Skills as `.foundry/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (directory-per-skill) — Option 2A The directory-per-skill layout mirrors what both Cursor and Claude Code already consume. It requires no new tooling, keeps content human-readable and git-reviewable, and allows co-location of per-skill auxiliary files. The manifest-generated approach (Option 2B) would introduce a build step and a new tool with no current consumer -- premature per ontology discipline. The canonical `SKILL.md` in `.foundry/skills/<name>/` contains the **environment-neutral procedure body** only. Environment-specific frontmatter (model routing, tool-specific keys like Cursor's `model:` or Claude Code's `effort:`) belongs exclusively in the overlay files under `.cursor/skills/<name>/` or `.claude/skills/<name>/`. ### Question 3: 30-day dual-read with structured logging — Option 3A The dual-read window provides a safe migration path without cross-platform symlink concerns. The 30-day window is long enough to cover typical sprint cycles and short enough to avoid indefinite technical debt. Structured `WARN`-level logging makes fallback usage observable so the team knows when the window can be closed early or must be extended. The dual-read applies only to **continuity instance paths** (project charters and `current-task.json`). Persona and skill paths do not need dual-read because they are being consolidated from `flagship-foundry-work/personas/` (not `.codex/`) and the environment overlay stubs will be updated in the same migration pass. ## Normative Layout After this decision, the canonical `.foundry/` tree is: ``` .foundry/ README.md # Layout guide and discovery contract schemas/ # Foundry-owned schemas (task-state, etc.) task-state.schema.json projects/ # Per-project continuity instances <slug>/ current-task.json # Runtime continuity (ADR-011) SDLC_CHARTER.md # Human-readable charter (ADR-011) personas/ # Repo-wide persona packs (NEW) <id>.json # e.g., ecosystem-orchestrator.json skills/ # Foundry-owned skill procedures (NEW) <name>/ SKILL.md # Canonical procedure body (env-neutral) agents/ # Foundry-owned agent definitions (NEW) <name>.md # Canonical role definition (env-neutral) ``` ### Reserved (do not create until a feature needs them) - `.foundry/cache/` - `.foundry/templates/` - `.foundry/projects/<slug>/persona-overrides/` ## Inheritance Model The inheritance model follows a **base + overlay** pattern: ``` .foundry/ <-- BASE (canonical, Foundry-owned) agents/<name>.md Full role definition, phase bindings, skills/<name>/SKILL.md forbidden behaviors, output contracts, personas/<id>.json procedure steps (environment-neutral) .cursor/ <-- OVERLAY (Cursor-specific adapter) agents/<name>.md Frontmatter: model routing (e.g., composer-2-fast) skills/<name>/SKILL.md + import/include of .foundry base content + Cursor-specific tool integrations .claude/ <-- OVERLAY (Claude Code-specific adapter) agents/<name>.md Frontmatter: model routing (e.g., opus) skills/<name>/SKILL.md + import/include of .foundry base content + Claude Code-specific tool integrations ``` **Rules:** 1. The `.foundry/` copy is the **single source of truth** for Foundry-behavioral content. 2. Overlay files in `.cursor/` and `.claude/` **must not duplicate** the canonical procedure body. They contain only: (a) tool-specific frontmatter, (b) a reference to the `.foundry/` base file, and (c) environment-specific extensions (e.g., tool-specific invocation syntax). 3. If an overlay file exists without a corresponding `.foundry/` base, it is a **tool-specific-only** artifact (not Foundry-owned) and is not subject to this ADR. 4. Persona JSON files have no overlay mechanism; they are consumed directly from `.foundry/personas/` by all environments. ## Dual-Read Migration Strategy **Scope**: Continuity instance paths only (`current-task.json`, `SDLC_CHARTER.md`). **Mechanism**: 1. `continuity.mjs` resolves project state by trying `.foundry/projects/<slug>/current-task.json` first. 2. On file-not-found, fall back to `.codex/projects/<slug>/current-task.json`. 3. On fallback hit, emit a structured warning: ``` WARN [continuity] Legacy path used: .codex/projects/<slug>/current-task.json Migrate to: .foundry/projects/<slug>/current-task.json Deprecation window closes: <merge-date + 30 days> ``` 4. The fallback code path is removed in a follow-up commit after 30 calendar days from the migration merge date. The removal date is tracked as a comment in the source and as a `derivedMirrors` entry in the continuity instance. **Not in scope for dual-read**: Personas (moving from `flagship-foundry-work/personas/`, not `.codex/`) and skills (overlay stubs updated in the same pass as the base files are created). ## Consequences ### Positive - Single canonical text for all 13 personas, 10 skills, and 8 agent definitions eliminates drift. - New environment integrations (e.g., a future Windsurf or VS Code agent) inherit Foundry behavior by reading `.foundry/` without copying content. - Flat persona layout keeps paths short and discovery simple. - Directory-per-skill preserves familiar structure and requires no new build tooling. - 30-day dual-read provides a safe, observable migration with a hard deadline. ### Negative - Overlay files in `.cursor/` and `.claude/` must be refactored from full copies to thin wrappers (one-time cost, bounded to wo-004). - Developers must know to edit `.foundry/` for canonical content, not the overlay -- requires team communication. - The 30-day window adds temporary code complexity in `continuity.mjs` (removed after window closes). ### Risks | Risk | Severity | Mitigation | |------|----------|------------| | Developers edit overlay instead of base, causing drift | Medium | CI lint rule: overlay files must not contain canonical body text (can be a grep-based check). Document in `.foundry/README.md`. | | Dual-read window expires before all consumers migrate | Low | The 30-day window can be extended with a documented justification commit. Logging makes usage observable. | | `.foundry/personas/` is too flat for future multi-tenancy | Low | Reserved `projects/<slug>/persona-overrides/` provides an escape hatch without restructuring. | | Environment tooling cannot resolve `@import` or `@include` from overlay to base | Medium | Overlay mechanism is tool-specific (Cursor uses `@file` references; Claude Code uses inline includes). Each adapter documents its own resolution strategy. If includes are not supported, the overlay contains a brief pointer comment and the full procedure is loaded at runtime from `.foundry/`. | ## References - `flagship-foundry-work/docs/adr/adr-011-foundry-directory-layout-and-continuity-instance.md` - `flagship-foundry-work/docs/adr/adr-002-continuity-schema-authority-and-bootstrap.md` - `flagship-foundry-work/docs/intent/intent-foundry-dot-foundry-ssot-charters-personas-skills-2026-03-23.md` - `flagship-foundry-work/docs/intent/scope-chunk-foundry-dot-foundry-ssot-charters-personas-skills-2026-03-23.md` - `flagship-foundry-work/schemas/persona-pack.schema.json` - `flagship-foundry-work/schemas/continuity-state.schema.json` - `flagship-foundry-work/packages/core/src/continuity.mjs`

===FILE:apps/flagship-foundry/docs/API_OVERVIEW.md===# Control Plane API Overview The control plane API is deliberately small. ## Endpoints - `GET /health` — health response and runtime graph path - `GET /graph` — return graph JSON - `POST /graph/patch` — apply graph patch operations - `POST /change-requests` — persist a change request envelope - `POST /orchestration/plan` — return a generated orchestration plan - `POST /telemetry/intake` — translate an incident into a change request - `GET /catalogs/runbooks` — list runbook metadata - `GET /catalogs/personas` — list persona metadata - `GET /catalogs/providers` — list provider metadata - `GET /catalogs/adapters` — list adapter metadata - `GET /catalogs/guardrails` — list guardrail metadata ## Design intent This API is not the final product API. It is the first stable contract that lets terminal agents, future IDE surfaces, and automated supervisors speak to a shared control plane. The API should remain: - implementation-light, - schema-driven, - provider-agnostic, - safe to wrap inside MCP or OpenAPI adapters later.
===FILE:apps/flagship-foundry/docs/BLAST_RADIUS_STRATEGY.md===# Blast Radius Strategy Your stated pain is real: plans can sound complete while silently skipping sibling surfaces, shared patterns, or parallel systems. Foundry addresses that with six blast-radius layers: 1. **Direct dependency graph** - imports, path aliases, and project references. 2. **Shared pattern graph** - same tags, same platform, same framework, same rule packs. 3. **Capability lineage** - service worker, content, side panel, popup, telemetry, storage, permissions, and other surfaced capabilities. 4. **Governance coupling** - if a rule pack, runbook, or contract changes, all governed projects are candidate impacts. 5. **Environment coupling** - if shared Cursor, Codex, Claude Code, or MCP doctrine changes, related workflows and adapters are candidate impacts. 6. **Operational evidence** - telemetry and defect clusters expand impact beyond current code touch points. ## Current minimum slice - `packages/core/src/blast-radius.mjs` calculates the scored impact set. - `packages/core/src/focus-views.mjs` turns a query into a drilldown Mermaid diagram. - risky plans can now insert adversarial challenge and reconciliation rounds before implementation. For MV3 ecosystems specifically, any service-worker change should review content scripts, popup, side panel, storage, permissions, and messaging contracts before execution proceeds.

===FILE:apps/flagship-foundry/docs/ci-release-gates.md===# CI baseline and release evidence threshold (ADR-009) This document is the operator-facing definition of **blocking automation** and **release evidence** for Flagship Foundry under [adr-009-ci-gate-baseline-and-release-evidence-threshold.md](adr/adr-009-ci-gate-baseline-and-release-evidence-threshold.md). ## Blocking CI baseline (minimum) When this repository is hosted on GitHub, the workflow **`.github/workflows/flagship-foundry-ci.yml`** (repo root) runs on changes under `flagship-foundry-work/`. | Gate | Command | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | **1** | `npm test` (from `flagship-foundry-work/`) | Full automated test surface (`node --test`). | | **2** | `npm run ci:targeted` | Non-unit path: orchestrator CLI `visualize` against the sample workspace (imports graph pipeline). | Local parity (run before push): ```bash cd flagship-foundry-work npm install npm test npm run ci:targeted ``` ## Inspectable evidence - **CI green status** is necessary but **not sufficient** for production-style release (ADR-009). - Each workflow run produces an artifact **`flagship-foundry-ci-gates-<run_id>`** containing `ci-gate-evidence.txt` with repository, run URL, commit SHA, and gate labels. Attach or reference this for milestone sign-off. - **Release readiness** also requires evidence that **M2** (classification, parity policy, knowledge/gap signals) and **M3** (auth boundary, telemetry correlation, adapter isolation) quality signals remain satisfied for the change scope—typically by referencing prior verifier packets, evidence bundles, or run-linked artifacts, not only the latest green CI run. ## Waivers and future gates Categories not yet automated (for example SBOM or dependency CVE gates) remain **explicit blockers** or **documented waivers** per ADR-009—they must not be treated as silent future work. ## Related - [source-of-truth-matrix.md](source-of-truth-matrix.md) — artifact authority - [REPOSITORY_LAYOUT.md](REPOSITORY_LAYOUT.md) — canonical app root - [NEXT_AGENT_EXECUTION_STEPS.md](adr/NEXT_AGENT_EXECUTION_STEPS.md) — agent verification playbook - [rollout-rollback-incident-model.md](rollout-rollback-incident-model.md) — go/no-go and operational linkage (ADR-010)
===FILE:apps/flagship-foundry/docs/COMPREHENSIVE_GUIDE.md===# Flagship Foundry: Comprehensive End-to-End Guide Welcome to **Flagship Foundry**, a graph-native Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) control plane designed for Visual-Driven Development (VDD) with Human + AI orchestration. This guide explains how the ecosystem works, the roles of each AI Agent, and the step-by-step order of operations to take a project from an initial idea to a fully verified, executed reality with minimal token cost and maximum reliability. --- ## 1. Core Philosophy: Visual-Driven Development Flagship Foundry shifts the developer experience from "reading thousands of lines of code" to **visual traversal and system overview**. You interact with your system via an interactive, split-pane IDE (the Cursor Companion). Diagrams are not just pictures—they are **executable indexes into design intent**. When you click a node on the visual graph, you navigate directly to the code. When you approve a node, it becomes an executable task for an AI. --- ## 2. Architecture Topology The Foundry ecosystem operates through the following interconnected layers: 1. **Foundry Control Plane (`apps/control-plane`)**: The brain of the operation. It maintains the system graph (AST), schemas, knowledge base, gap analysis, and the approval engine. 2. **Foundry MCP Server (`apps/foundry-mcp-server`)**: Exposes the Foundry Control Plane to external Runtimes (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) using the standard Model Context Protocol. 3. **Model Gateway (`packages/model-gateway`)**: Normalizes all AI model requests. It routes high-reasoning tasks to Anthropic/MiniMax and low-cost execution tasks to a local SSH-tunneled model (Qwen3-Coder). 4. **Interactive Cockpit (`apps/cursor-companion`)**: The VS Code/Cursor extension that renders the dynamic Mermaid logic graph, highlights blast radii, and provides execution controls (Approve/Start/Pause/Stop). 5. **Ralph Execution Loop (`packages/core/src/ralph-`...)**: The autonomous executor loop that continuously processes bounded microtasks deterministically without reinventing the architecture. --- ## 3. The AI Agent Swarm (Roles) Your development pipeline is fulfilled by a Swarm Consensus Model. Different models play different roles to ensure structural integrity: * **The Specifier (MiniMax / Claude):** Intake. Translates your human requirement into formal capability statements, constraints, and risk posture. * **The Architect (MiniMax / Claude):** Generates the initial system diagram, state flow, and bounded PRD Shards based on the Specifier's requirements. * **The Adversary (Separate High-Reasoning Model):** Attacks the Architect's diagram. Identifies hidden blast radiuses, tight coupling, and rollback concerns. Forces a Reconciler phase if vulnerabilities are found. * **The Verifier (Codex):** A disciplined reviewer that checks the final PRD shard for completeness and strict verification logic before declaring it "Ready for Execution." * **The Builder / Ralph (Qwen-3 Coder):** The cheap, deterministic, local/tunneled executor that blindly loops through authorized PRD components one at a time. It updates `progress.txt` and learns from its execution failures. --- ## 4. End-to-End Project Development Lifecycle (The Workflow) When you begin a new project (or ingest a new feature for an existing ecosystem), you will follow this exact pipeline: ### Step 1: Ingestion & Environment Bootstrapping Before any code is written, the system must understand what exists. 1. **Start the Control Plane & MCP Server.** 2. **Import Workspace:** The control plane parses your directory and turns it into a System Graph. 3. **Ingest Seed Knowledge:** Documentation, framework rules, and domain heuristics are loaded into the Knowledge Base. 4. **Analyze Gaps:** The system highlights what your current setup is missing (e.g., missing React UI guidelines, missing security protocols) so agents do not hallucinate. ### Step 2: Requirement Capture & Diagram Synthesis 1. You describe a feature objective via the **Cursor Companion Overlay**. 2. The **Specifier** and **Architect** are invoked. They build a proposed Component Architecture. 3. The **Interactive Focus Graph** dynamically renders in your IDE beside your code. ### Step 3: Adversarial Debate & Blast Radius Discovery 1. The Foundry orchestrator automatically feeds the proposed Graph to the **Adversary**. 2. The Adversary highlights nodes that will break (blast radius). 3. The Architect updates the design safely. 4. If the risk is high, the system pauses. **Human Approval Gates** require you to click "Approve" on the revised diagram via the Webview. ### Step 4: Sharding & Ralph Bridge Execution 1. Once Approved, the system compiles the visual nodes into **Executable PRD Shards** (`prd.json`, `AGENTS.md`). 2. The **Foundry-to-Ralph** compiler spins up local workspaces for these shards. 3. You click **"Start Run"** in the Cursor UI. 4. **Ralph (Qwen3-Coder)** begins grinding through the shards locally. ### Step 5: Sync & Verification 1. As Ralph completes tasks, `progress.txt` is updated. 2. **Ralph State Sync** automatically pushes updates back into the Foundry Graph. 3. The visual node in your IDE turns green. 4. The **Verifier** runs unit tests. If tests pass, the feature is successfully integrated! --- ## 5. Standard Operating Procedures (What to do in what order) To manually operate the minimal slice of the ecosystem today, follow these sequenced events via your terminal or IDE: **1. Start the Foundation** Open the integrated terminal and start the Control Plane API: \`\`\`bash npm run api \`\`\` *(Optional) Ensure you start `foundry-mcp-server` and `model-gateway` out of their respective app folders.* **2. Open your Cockpit** In VS Code / Cursor, run the command **`Flagship Foundry: Open Orchestration Overlay`**. This opens the split-pane View. **3. Run the Initialization Pipeline via the UI** In the Webview Overlay, click the buttons in this specific sequence: 1. `Start Plane` (Validates Health) 2. `Import` (Generates Ecosystem Manifest and initial Graph) 3. `Gap Analysis` (Determines missing documentation required for tasks) **4. Plan your Work (Visual Mapping)** 1. Click `Plan`. Type your objective (e.g., "Add user authentication flow"). 2. Click `Generate Focus Graph`. The Mermaid AST will render. You can click on the visual nodes to open specific source files instantly. **5. Execute and Monitor** 1. Review the generated "Latest Plan" block matching your objective. 2. Click `Approve` to satisfy the verification gate. 3. Click `Start Run`. 4. Monitor the "Latest Run (Ralph loop)" tab. Use `Pause` or `Stop` to interject if the agent loops unexpectedly. 5. Click `Refresh` to observe the progress bridging back from Ralph to your visual map!

===FILE:apps/flagship-foundry/docs/CURSOR_EXTENSION_BOOTSTRAP.md===# Cursor Companion Bootstrap The first editor surface is a VS Code-compatible companion intended to run inside Cursor while the control plane stays editor-agnostic. ## What the companion does - starts the local control plane from the current workspace; - imports the current workspace into Foundry; - ingests the seed knowledge manifest; - runs gap analysis against the imported ecosystem; - creates draft plans from a short objective; - opens a focused blast-radius drilldown view; - approves plans or starts runs; - pauses, resumes, and stops the latest run. ## Why this is the right first surface It gives you plan visibility, knowledge quality feedback, and execution controls inside the editor you are already using, while preserving the deeper long-term path toward a dedicated orchestration shell. ## Extension folder - `apps/cursor-companion/package.json` - `apps/cursor-companion/extension.js` Install the extension from that folder in a VS Code-compatible environment and point it at the same workspace that contains the Foundry control plane.
===FILE:apps/flagship-foundry/docs/docker-and-local-dev.md===# Docker and local development ## Default: no Docker required For most contributors, run **Node.js on the host** from `flagship-foundry-work/`: - `npm install`, `npm test`, `npm run api`, orchestrator CLI — all expect direct filesystem access to the repo and `state/`. ## Optional: containerize the control plane **When it helps** - CI pipelines that need a **reproducible** Node version and dependency install - Teams that want a **single command** to start the HTTP API with pinned deps **Typical pattern** - Build an image that contains `flagship-foundry-work` (or install from lockfile) - Expose the control-plane port (per `apps/control-plane` defaults) - Mount **read/write** only what is required; **never** bake secrets into images **Security (ADR-006)** - Non-loopback access requires **bearer tokens** and scoped CORS - Pass `FLAGSHIP_CONTROL_PLANE_BEARER_TOKEN` and related env via **env files or secrets**, not committed config ## What usually stays on the host - **Orchestrator CLI** — needs direct paths to customer repos for `filesystem` import - **Local-shell execute runs** — isolation and sandbox behavior differ by OS (**ADR-008**); Docker is not a substitute for that policy without a dedicated design ## What may be containerized later - **Graph viewer** dev server (`apps/graph-viewer`) if teams use it in shared demos - **MCP server** (`apps/foundry-mcp-server`) for isolated dependency sets ## Summary | Component | Default | Container optional? | |-----------|---------|---------------------| | CLI + tests | Host | No | | Control plane API | Host | Yes | | CI gates (`npm test`, `ci:targeted`) | Host / CI runner | Yes |
===FILE:apps/flagship-foundry/docs/ENVIRONMENT_PARITY_AND_MIGRATION.md===# Environment Parity and Migration ## Principle Cursor, Codex, Claude Code, Gemini, local models, and future runtimes should all consume the same project doctrine and work-order contract. Tool-specific files are projections of that intent, not separate systems of truth. ## Current parity templates - `environments/cursor/project/` - `environments/codex/project/` - `environments/claude/project/` ## Current scaffold command ```bash node apps/orchestrator-cli/src/main.mjs scaffold-env cursor-project ./some-target --dry-run ``` ## What parity should cover - approval defaults; - shared MCP servers; - project doctrine and guardrails; - runbook references; - local model routing or gateway endpoints; - task result and evidence expectations. ## Migration posture Foundry should detect what already exists in `.cursor`, `.claude`, `.codex`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and `.mcp.json`, then show what is missing rather than overwriting working setups blindly.
===FILE:apps/flagship-foundry/docs/flagship_agentic_ecosystem_spec.md===# Flagship Graph-Native Agentic SDLC Ecosystem Working name: **Flagship Foundry** ## Thesis Your materials already imply the architecture. This platform should **not** be built as a better chat interface, and **not** as a standalone diagram tool. It should be built as a **graph-native definition and evidence engine** where: - humans own intent, scope, ethics, constraints, risk tolerance, and approval boundaries; - AI agents perform transformation work inside declared guardrails; - every meaningful decision produces an artifact; - every artifact has an owner, source of truth, and update rule; - every phase is gated by evidence rather than ceremony; - every runtime is observable, diagnosable, and recoverable; - every completed task leaves behind deterministic continuity for the next pass. That makes the product a living digital twin of: 1. **declared intent**, 2. **implemented reality**, 3. **runtime evidence**, and 4. **learned guardrails**. ## Product statement The ecosystem continuously transforms: **idea -> definitions -> diagrams -> contracts -> work orders -> code/tests/config -> evidence -> learning -> better guardrails** The orchestrator does not think in prompts. It thinks in: - lifecycle stage, - authority stack, - graph state, - work-order contracts, - verification evidence, - approvals, - rollback posture, - and cost-aware model routing. ## What makes this different ### 1. One system graph, many views The core system of record is a property graph, not a folder of disconnected files. That graph renders multiple views without duplicating truth: - context diagram - system landscape - container diagram - component diagram - dynamic / sequence view - deployment diagram - data flow diagram - event flow diagram - trust boundary diagram - observability map - ownership map - failure / recovery diagram - production runtime flow dashboard ### 2. Typed task decomposition Every change becomes a tree of typed work orders: - ecosystem-level intent - system-level impact plans - component-level implementation plans - file-level execution tasks - verification tasks - release tasks - learning tasks Each work order has a bounded context budget, explicit inputs, explicit outputs, allowed tools, validation rules, approval requirements, and a deterministic handoff. ### 3. Model-cost optimization by task class The orchestrator uses expensive models only for ambiguity-heavy work: - architectural reasoning - impact analysis - tradeoff selection - failure diagnosis - incident triage - policy interpretation It uses low-cost models or deterministic executors for narrow work: - code edits against a known contract - unit-test expansion - documentation synchronization - schema upgrades - rule-pack application - formatting / refactoring inside known boundaries ### 4. Operate-to-improve feedback loop Telemetry, incidents, regressions, and postmortems are not external to development. They become graph evidence that can: - identify impacted systems, - trigger system orchestrators, - generate remediation work orders, - update risk models, - propose guardrail-pack changes, - and improve future execution. ## Non-negotiable product invariants 1. **Human intent remains authoritative.** 2. **No silent mutation of the source of truth.** 3. **Every artifact is attributable to a task, phase, or decision.** 4. **Verification agents must be able to disagree with builder agents.** 5. **Release decisions must consume evidence, not assumptions.** 6. **Context is minimized per microtask and reset after completion.** 7. **Extracted evidence and declared truth remain distinguishable.** 8. **All high-risk actions require policy or human approval.** 9. **Continuity state must be reconstructible from committed artifacts only.** 10. **The graph is the shared semantic substrate across design, build, and operations.** ## System planes ### A. Experience plane User-facing modes: - Founder / product mode - Architect mode - Engineering mode - Operator / SRE mode - Learning mode - Portfolio / leadership mode Interfaces: - guided question flow - graph canvas - artifact workspace - task board - diff / approval panel - production visualization dashboard - incident cockpit - learning replay mode ### B. Definition plane This plane produces structured intent artifacts: - problem statement - glossary - success metrics - scope / non-goals - acceptance criteria - risks - ADRs - contracts and schemas - diagrams - rollout plan - observability plan - maintenance plan ### C. Graph plane The graph stores declared, inferred, and measured reality. #### Core node types - Ecosystem - Portfolio - System - Capability - UserRole - Stakeholder - Team - Component - Module - File - Runtime - Environment - DeploymentUnit - DataObject - DataStore - API - Event - Contract - Schema - Feature - ChangeRequest - Task - WorkOrder - TestSuite - EvidenceBundle - Incident - Alert - SLO - Risk - GuardrailPack - DecisionRecord - Owner #### Core edge types - CONTAINS - DEPENDS_ON - IMPLEMENTS - OWNS - EMITS - CONSUMES - CALLS - READS - WRITES - DEPLOYS_TO - VERIFIED_BY - GATED_BY - IMPACTS - DERIVED_FROM - BLOCKED_BY - SUPERSEDES - LEARNS_FROM - CONSTRAINED_BY - APPROVED_BY #### Provenance classes - declared - generated - inferred - observed - imported - learned Each node and edge should support: - provenance - confidence - owner - authority - last_verified_at - source_artifacts[] - evidence_refs[] - supersedes / superseded_by ### D. Orchestration plane This is the control brain. #### Orchestration hierarchy 1. **Ecosystem Orchestrator** - owns global intent translation - determines impacted systems - sets cost/risk posture - approves or rejects system plans 2. **System Orchestrator** - understands a single system boundary - decomposes change into component work streams - manages system-local continuity and evidence 3. **Component Orchestrator** - maps requirements to contracts, files, tests, and migrations - emits file-scoped or module-scoped work orders 4. **Execution Agents** - builder - verifier - security reviewer - performance reviewer - docs/release agent - migration/data agent - incident/diagnostic agent ### E. Execution plane Execution agents should run inside isolated work contexts with: - minimal source packet - approved tools only - persona pack + guardrail pack - explicit success criteria - rollback / abort behavior - post-task state writeback ### F. Evidence plane This plane ingests: - source control diffs - CI results - build artifacts - test results - coverage - OpenAPI / AsyncAPI / JSON Schema contracts - IaC state - telemetry - alerts - traces - logs - incidents - postmortems - SBOM / provenance artifacts ### G. Learning plane This plane converts repeated evidence into reusable operating knowledge: - known failure patterns - anti-patterns - framework-specific guardrails - environment-specific runbooks - incident classes - remediation playbooks - maturity scoring - suggested standards updates ## Agent taxonomy ### Core planner / curator roles - **Intent Curator** - cleans human request into a change envelope - **Context Curator** - assembles source packet and evidence bundle - **Impact Analyst** - determines affected systems, contracts, and runtimes - **Systems Architect** - emits structure, boundaries, and ADR candidates ### Execution roles - **Builder** - code/config/IaC implementation - **Contract Agent** - schema/API/event contract creation and synchronization - **Migration Agent** - state/data/config transitions - **UI Experience Agent** - interface, flow, and accessibility alignment - **Test Agent** - unit/integration/E2E/perf/security test production ### Independent reviewer roles - **Verifier** - compares expected versus actual behavior - **Security Reviewer** - checks trust boundaries, secrets, supply chain, authz - **Performance Reviewer** - checks latency, throughput, churn, memory, stability - **Compliance Reviewer** - validates SSDF/ASVS/policy mappings ### Operational roles - **Release Agent** - release note assembly, rollout execution, rollback readiness - **SRE / Diagnostics Agent** - incident triage and evidence packaging - **Learning Agent** - postmortem mining and guardrail updates ## Persona packs versus role packs Your idea of “different agent personalities” is valid, but it should be formalized. Do **not** treat personality as vibe or style. Treat it as a **behavior profile** layered on top of a role. ### Role pack Defines: - job to be done - allowed tools - required inputs - required outputs - acceptance rules - escalation behavior ### Persona pack Defines: - skepticism level - verbosity level - bias toward caution vs speed - tolerance for assumption-making - formatting discipline - evidence threshold - fallback behavior Examples: - **Architect persona:** broad, exploratory, tradeoff-aware, asks for ambiguity reduction - **Builder persona:** conservative, exact, contract-first, low-creativity - **Verifier persona:** adversarial, skeptical, independent - **Security persona:** least-privilege, zero-trust, evidence-heavy - **Docs persona:** terse, authoritative, synchronization-focused ## Task classes and model routing | Task class | Typical work | Preferred execution tier | |---|---|---| | Strategic reasoning | architecture, tradeoffs, system decomposition | high-reasoning model | | Constraint interpretation | policy mapping, compliance, runtime safety | high-reasoning or balanced model | | Deterministic transformation | code patching, refactor, doc sync | low-cost executor | | Structured generation | tests, schemas, manifests, boilerplate | low-cost executor | | Verification | run/compare/assert/evidence summarize | separate verifier model or deterministic tools | | Diagnostics | incident triage, impact isolation | high-reasoning model with evidence bundle | | Learning | mine postmortems, update packs | balanced model + human approval | ### Routing rules - High ambiguity -> high reasoning. - High blast radius -> high reasoning + approval. - Narrow contract-constrained change -> low-cost executor. - Repeated known fix class -> rules engine or very small model. - Verification must not share hidden state with builder execution. ## Work-order contract Every executable unit should conform to a common work-order schema. Required fields: - work_order_id - parent_work_order_id - lifecycle_stage - phase_id - system_id - component_id (optional) - task_class - agent_role - agent_persona - model_tier - context_budget - source_artifacts[] - input_graph_refs[] - allowed_tools[] - constraints[] - expected_outputs[] - acceptance_criteria[] - verification_plan[] - rollback_notes - escalation_rules - approval_requirements - status - evidence_refs[] - graph_patch - continuity_patch ## Continuity model The ecosystem should preserve state at two levels: ### 1. Lifecycle state Where is the system in the universal SDLC? - discover - define - visualize - architect - plan - implement - verify - release - operate - diagnose - improve ### 2. Phase execution state What exact checkpoint is active right now? Examples: - phase-10-stabilization-settings-authority - platform-shell-workspace - proof-regression-hardening - release-canary-1 ### Important correction from your current artifacts Your current continuity assets reveal a concrete schema mismatch: - `task-state.schema.json` constrains `sdlcPhase` to broad lifecycle values. - `current-task.json` currently uses a specific phase slug (`phase-10-stabilization-settings-authority`). That means the present schema cannot fully represent the checkpoint style your real work already uses. **Fix:** split the field into: - `lifecycleStage` -> strict enum for the universal SDLC - `phaseId` -> free-form slug for the exact checkpoint I included that correction in the new continuity schema artifact. ## Guardrail-pack architecture To support framework-agnostic execution, guardrails must be modular. ### Pack types - **Language pack** - TypeScript, Python, Go, Rust, Java, etc. - **Framework pack** - React, Next, FastAPI, Spring, Nest, Vue, Angular, etc. - **Cloud pack** - AWS, Azure, GCP, Cloudflare, Vercel, Kubernetes, serverless, etc. - **Compliance pack** - HIPAA, SOC 2, PCI, GDPR, internal policy - **Repo pack** - local conventions, build/test commands, folder boundaries - **System pack** - one system’s known quirks, failure modes, standards, and runbooks ### Pack contents Each pack should contain: - doctrine and invariants - allowed / disallowed patterns - templates - examples - required checks - quality gates - error taxonomy - known failure classes - remediation playbooks - escalation triggers - output format requirements - test obligations ### Pack lifecycle 1. ingest docs / source / standards 2. interpret into structured pack format 3. human approve 4. assign semantic version 5. attach to systems and agents 6. learn from incidents and update with review ## Three primary operating loops ### Loop 1: intent -> architecture 1. human defines mission, constraints, scope, success metrics 2. question engine fills missing structure 3. graph updates in real time 4. diagrams render automatically 5. gates detect missing artifacts 6. orchestrator proposes first implementation slice ### Loop 2: architecture -> implementation 1. ecosystem orchestrator identifies impacted systems 2. system orchestrators create work trees 3. work orders are model-routed 4. agents execute with bounded context 5. outputs are verified independently 6. graph and artifacts are updated 7. context resets to baseline with state persisted ### Loop 3: operate -> improve 1. runtime telemetry or incident enters evidence plane 2. graph impact analysis finds touched systems/components 3. system orchestrators propose remediation plan 4. approved remediation emits work orders 5. fixes, tests, runbooks, diagrams, and packs update together 6. learning agent proposes new standards or reusable fixes ## Gate evaluation as graph queries ### Definition of Ready A change is DoR-green only when the graph can answer yes to: - does a goal exist? - are measurable acceptance criteria linked? - are risks captured? - is a rollback idea attached? - does a test outline exist? ### Definition of Done DoD is green only when: - linked acceptance criteria passed - verification evidence exists - docs and diagrams updated - operational impact reviewed ### Release gate Release is green only when: - build artifacts exist - environment configuration validated - staged verification green - rollback path rehearsed or approved ### Operate gate Production readiness is green only when: - owner assigned - telemetry exists - alerts exist - dashboards exist - runbooks exist - baseline / rollback point exists ## Experience design and animation model Your “fun, interactive, animated diagram” idea should be a first-class experience mode, not a gimmick. ### Visualization modes - **Engineering mode:** precise, dense, operationally accurate - **Learning mode:** simplified labels, guided tours, glossary overlays, causal animations - **Operations mode:** production traffic, incidents, alerts, SLO posture - **Portfolio mode:** system-to-system landscape and blast radius ### Animation principles - edge pulses represent runtime events or data flow - node glow indicates change, incident, deploy, drift, or approval pending - timing is sourced from real event timestamps where possible - spacing and motion prioritize clarity over spectacle - user can switch between “diagram truth” and “runtime truth” layers ### Learning mode goals - teach system structure to juniors and non-engineers - make dependencies and state transitions visible - reduce jargon through graph-linked glossary definitions - support classroom or onboarding walkthroughs ## Recommended initial implementation stack Use the stack your graph-driven analysis already identified unless you have a stronger house preference: - question flow/statecharts: XState - answer validation/contracts: JSON Schema - schema-driven UI: JSON Forms or SurveyJS - graph canvas: Cytoscape.js + ELK - diagrams: C4 + Structurizr + Mermaid - code intelligence: tree-sitter + SCIP/LSIF where needed - security analysis: CodeQL and/or Semgrep - supply-chain evidence: SLSA + SPDX/CycloneDX The platform should remain host-agnostic and orchestration-runtime-agnostic. OpenClaw can be one possible orchestrator host, but the architecture itself should not depend on any single agent shell. ## MVP definition ### MVP-1: Definition engine Deliver these first: - guided question flow - graph store - real-time graph projection - context/container/deployment/observability artifact generation - glossary + ADR + acceptance-criteria generators - DoR / DoD / Release / Operate gate evaluator - continuity state with deterministic resume ### MVP-2: Orchestrated implementation Then add: - work-order schema and queue - model routing - system orchestrators - builder / verifier / docs agents - artifact diff + evidence bundle generation - file-level execution with resettable context ### MVP-3: Operate / diagnose / improve Then add: - telemetry ingestion - graph impact analysis from incidents - remediation plan generation - runtime visualization dashboard - learning agent and guardrail updates ### MVP-4: Multi-tenant productization Finally add: - multi-workspace tenancy - approvals and review workflows - compliance packs - shared pack registry - portfolio view and maturity scoring ## Build order for your ecosystem ### Phase 0 - foundation - define doctrine - finalize graph ontology - finalize continuity schema v2 - finalize work-order schema - define agent role packs and persona packs ### Phase 1 - definition and visualization - build question engine - build graph projection - build first diagram generator set - build gate evaluator ### Phase 2 - execution control - add work-order generation - add orchestrator hierarchy - add builder/verifier/docs agents - add evidence bundle writer ### Phase 3 - runtime evidence - ingest CI, tests, telemetry, incidents - create impact analysis - create operational dashboard ### Phase 4 - learning system - mine repeated defects - produce reusable system packs - propose standards changes and approval workflows ## The first thing I would fix in your existing assets 1. Split `sdlcPhase` into `lifecycleStage` and `phaseId`. 2. Standardize a reusable work-order schema. 3. Add graph revision IDs to continuity state. 4. Make artifact authority explicit per artifact class. 5. Distinguish declared truth, inferred truth, and observed truth in the graph. 6. Require every agent completion to emit both a graph patch and a continuity patch. ## Success criteria for the platform The ecosystem is working when it can do all of the following reliably: - a novice can describe a system without choosing a framework first; - the graph renders the right diagrams as answers arrive; - a multi-system change is decomposed into typed work orders; - low-cost agents complete narrow tasks without broad context; - verification catches builder mistakes; - incidents generate targeted remediation plans; - repeated failures improve packs and standards; - a paused session can be resumed from committed artifacts alone. ## Final recommendation Build this as a **graph-native control plane for human-owned intent and AI-executed transformation**. That gives you the exact shape your materials point toward: - framework agnostic - evidence driven - phase aware - resumable - guardrailed - model-cost efficient - visually rich - and capable of evolving from design tool -> orchestrator -> operational digital twin -> learning environment.
===FILE:apps/flagship-foundry/docs/FOUNDRY_ECOSYSTEM_SPEC.md===# Flagship Graph-Native Agentic SDLC Ecosystem Working name: **Flagship Foundry** ## Thesis Your materials already imply the architecture. This platform should **not** be built as a better chat interface, and **not** as a standalone diagram tool. It should be built as a **graph-native definition and evidence engine** where: - humans own intent, scope, ethics, constraints, risk tolerance, and approval boundaries; - AI agents perform transformation work inside declared guardrails; - every meaningful decision produces an artifact; - every artifact has an owner, source of truth, and update rule; - every phase is gated by evidence rather than ceremony; - every runtime is observable, diagnosable, and recoverable; - every completed task leaves behind deterministic continuity for the next pass. That makes the product a living digital twin of: 1. **declared intent**, 2. **implemented reality**, 3. **runtime evidence**, and 4. **learned guardrails**. ## Product statement The ecosystem continuously transforms: **idea -> definitions -> diagrams -> contracts -> work orders -> code/tests/config -> evidence -> learning -> better guardrails** The orchestrator does not think in prompts. It thinks in: - lifecycle stage, - authority stack, - graph state, - work-order contracts, - verification evidence, - approvals, - rollback posture, - and cost-aware model routing. ## What makes this different ### 1. One system graph, many views The core system of record is a property graph, not a folder of disconnected files. That graph renders multiple views without duplicating truth: - context diagram - system landscape - container diagram - component diagram - dynamic / sequence view - deployment diagram - data flow diagram - event flow diagram - trust boundary diagram - observability map - ownership map - failure / recovery diagram - production runtime flow dashboard ### 2. Typed task decomposition Every change becomes a tree of typed work orders: - ecosystem-level intent - system-level impact plans - component-level implementation plans - file-level execution tasks - verification tasks - release tasks - learning tasks Each work order has a bounded context budget, explicit inputs, explicit outputs, allowed tools, validation rules, approval requirements, and a deterministic handoff. ### 3. Model-cost optimization by task class The orchestrator uses expensive models only for ambiguity-heavy work: - architectural reasoning - impact analysis - tradeoff selection - failure diagnosis - incident triage - policy interpretation It uses low-cost models or deterministic executors for narrow work: - code edits against a known contract - unit-test expansion - documentation synchronization - schema upgrades - rule-pack application - formatting / refactoring inside known boundaries ### 4. Operate-to-improve feedback loop Telemetry, incidents, regressions, and postmortems are not external to development. They become graph evidence that can: - identify impacted systems, - trigger system orchestrators, - generate remediation work orders, - update risk models, - propose guardrail-pack changes, - and improve future execution. ## Non-negotiable product invariants 1. **Human intent remains authoritative.** 2. **No silent mutation of the source of truth.** 3. **Every artifact is attributable to a task, phase, or decision.** 4. **Verification agents must be able to disagree with builder agents.** 5. **Release decisions must consume evidence, not assumptions.** 6. **Context is minimized per microtask and reset after completion.** 7. **Extracted evidence and declared truth remain distinguishable.** 8. **All high-risk actions require policy or human approval.** 9. **Continuity state must be reconstructible from committed artifacts only.** 10. **The graph is the shared semantic substrate across design, build, and operations.** ## System planes ### A. Experience plane User-facing modes: - Founder / product mode - Architect mode - Engineering mode - Operator / SRE mode - Learning mode - Portfolio / leadership mode Interfaces: - guided question flow - graph canvas - artifact workspace - task board - diff / approval panel - production visualization dashboard - incident cockpit - learning replay mode ### B. Definition plane This plane produces structured intent artifacts: - problem statement - glossary - success metrics - scope / non-goals - acceptance criteria - risks - ADRs - contracts and schemas - diagrams - rollout plan - observability plan - maintenance plan ### C. Graph plane The graph stores declared, inferred, and measured reality. #### Core node types - Ecosystem - Portfolio - System - Capability - UserRole - Stakeholder - Team - Component - Module - File - Runtime - Environment - DeploymentUnit - DataObject - DataStore - API - Event - Contract - Schema - Feature - ChangeRequest - Task - WorkOrder - TestSuite - EvidenceBundle - Incident - Alert - SLO - Risk - GuardrailPack - DecisionRecord - Owner #### Core edge types - CONTAINS - DEPENDS_ON - IMPLEMENTS - OWNS - EMITS - CONSUMES - CALLS - READS - WRITES - DEPLOYS_TO - VERIFIED_BY - GATED_BY - IMPACTS - DERIVED_FROM - BLOCKED_BY - SUPERSEDES - LEARNS_FROM - CONSTRAINED_BY - APPROVED_BY #### Provenance classes - declared - generated - inferred - observed - imported - learned Each node and edge should support: - provenance - confidence - owner - authority - last_verified_at - source_artifacts[] - evidence_refs[] - supersedes / superseded_by ### D. Orchestration plane This is the control brain. #### Orchestration hierarchy 1. **Ecosystem Orchestrator** - owns global intent translation - determines impacted systems - sets cost/risk posture - approves or rejects system plans 2. **System Orchestrator** - understands a single system boundary - decomposes change into component work streams - manages system-local continuity and evidence 3. **Component Orchestrator** - maps requirements to contracts, files, tests, and migrations - emits file-scoped or module-scoped work orders 4. **Execution Agents** - builder - verifier - security reviewer - performance reviewer - docs/release agent - migration/data agent - incident/diagnostic agent ### E. Execution plane Execution agents should run inside isolated work contexts with: - minimal source packet - approved tools only - persona pack + guardrail pack - explicit success criteria - rollback / abort behavior - post-task state writeback ### F. Evidence plane This plane ingests: - source control diffs - CI results - build artifacts - test results - coverage - OpenAPI / AsyncAPI / JSON Schema contracts - IaC state - telemetry - alerts - traces - logs - incidents - postmortems - SBOM / provenance artifacts ### G. Learning plane This plane converts repeated evidence into reusable operating knowledge: - known failure patterns - anti-patterns - framework-specific guardrails - environment-specific runbooks - incident classes - remediation playbooks - maturity scoring - suggested standards updates ## Agent taxonomy ### Core planner / curator roles - **Intent Curator** - cleans human request into a change envelope - **Context Curator** - assembles source packet and evidence bundle - **Impact Analyst** - determines affected systems, contracts, and runtimes - **Systems Architect** - emits structure, boundaries, and ADR candidates ### Execution roles - **Builder** - code/config/IaC implementation - **Contract Agent** - schema/API/event contract creation and synchronization - **Migration Agent** - state/data/config transitions - **UI Experience Agent** - interface, flow, and accessibility alignment - **Test Agent** - unit/integration/E2E/perf/security test production ### Independent reviewer roles - **Verifier** - compares expected versus actual behavior - **Security Reviewer** - checks trust boundaries, secrets, supply chain, authz - **Performance Reviewer** - checks latency, throughput, churn, memory, stability - **Compliance Reviewer** - validates SSDF/ASVS/policy mappings ### Operational roles - **Release Agent** - release note assembly, rollout execution, rollback readiness - **SRE / Diagnostics Agent** - incident triage and evidence packaging - **Learning Agent** - postmortem mining and guardrail updates ## Persona packs versus role packs Your idea of “different agent personalities” is valid, but it should be formalized. Do **not** treat personality as vibe or style. ===FILE:apps/flagship-foundry/docs/FOUNDRY_KNOWLEDGE_PIPELINE.md===# Foundry Knowledge Pipeline ## Purpose The knowledge pipeline exists to prevent the orchestrator from planning against vague intuition or tool-specific folklore. It turns documentation, local exports, framework references, and future downloaded doc bundles into versioned, attributable, reusable knowledge. ## Core flow 1. collect source manifests; 2. ingest and split sources into documents; 3. tag documents to domain packs, frameworks, and platforms; 4. publish a knowledge-base manifest and coverage report; 5. run ecosystem-aware gap analysis; 6. use the resulting recommendations to refine personas, runbooks, guardrails, skills, and environment parity. ## Source types in the current slice - combined markdown docs; - text bundles exported from existing repos; - JavaScript or source files treated as canonical tooling references. ## Current foundational sources - Claude Code docs bundle; - OpenAI Codex docs bundle; - Cursor learning-path bundle; - generic documentation scraper bundle; - Nx context bundler source. ## Why this matters The knowledge base is not a generic RAG dump. It is mapped to domain packs, framework registries, persona expectations, runbooks, and guardrails so the orchestrator can ask: what is missing for this ecosystem to plan and execute reliably?
===FILE:apps/flagship-foundry/docs/guides/cursor-extension-foundry-init.md===# Cursor / VS Code extension: Foundry init and re-init This document describes how a **local VS Code–compatible extension** (runs in Cursor) can support **initialize** and **re-initialize** workflows without replacing the orchestrator CLI. ## Feasible capabilities - **Commands** registered in `package.json` (e.g. “Foundry: Init project”, “Foundry: Import ecosystem”, “Foundry: Start control plane”). - **Spawn terminal or subprocess**: `node flagship-foundry-work/apps/orchestrator-cli/src/main.mjs init-project my-project "objective"` with `cwd` set to the **workspace folder** where `.foundry` should appear. - **Configuration**: `flagshipFoundry.controlPlaneUrl`, `flagshipFoundry.foundryRoot`, paths to import configs. - **Health check**: `fetch` to `GET /health` on the control plane before actions that require the API. ## Integration points - **CLI**: `apps/orchestrator-cli/src/main.mjs` — same surface as `npm run` scripts in `package.json`. - **Control plane**: `npm run api` from `flagship-foundry-work/`. - **Existing extension**: `apps/cursor-companion/` — extend with new commands rather than forking unrelated code. ## Non-goals - **No blind overwrite** of user-owned files (**ADR-004**). Re-init flows that touch skills, rules, or parity projections must use **dry-run**, **diff**, or **explicit approval**. - **No dependency** on undocumented Cursor-internal CLIs. - **Secrets** are not written into `.foundry/`; use environment or secure storage for tokens (**ADR-006**). ## Recommended UX 1. Prompt for **project slug** and **objective** → run `init-project`. 2. Optional: open **import config** picker → run `import` / `visualize`. 3. Optional: start **control plane** in a dedicated terminal if not already running. ## References - `apps/cursor-companion/README.md` - [ecosystem-onboarding.md](ecosystem-onboarding.md)
===FILE:apps/flagship-foundry/docs/guides/ecosystem-onboarding.md===# Ecosystem onboarding (step-by-step) Use this guide to bring a **real repository** into Flagship Foundry as an ecosystem and wire **continuity**, **knowledge**, and **verification**. Canonical app commands assume `cd flagship-foundry-work`. ## Prerequisites - Node.js 20+ - `npm install` in `flagship-foundry-work/` ## 1. Create an import request Save a JSON file (e.g. `my-ecosystem.import.json`) at a path you can pass to the CLI: ```json { "ecosystemId": "my-product", "name": "My Product", "source": { "type": "filesystem", "workspaceRoot": "/absolute/path/to/target/repo" } } ``` `workspaceRoot` must be the root of the codebase you want modeled. ## 2. Import the workspace ```bash node apps/orchestrator-cli/src/main.mjs import /path/to/my-ecosystem.import.json ``` **Outputs:** `state/ecosystems/<ecosystemId>/` (manifest, graph, reports). ## 3. Visualize (optional) ```bash node apps/orchestrator-cli/src/main.mjs visualize /path/to/my-ecosystem.import.json ``` ## 4. Ingest knowledge (recommended) Use or adapt a manifest under `examples/knowledge-sources/` as a template, then: ```bash node apps/orchestrator-cli/src/main.mjs knowledge /path/to/manifest.json ``` ## 5. Gap analysis Prepare a gap request JSON referencing `ecosystemId` and `knowledgeBaseId` as needed (see `examples/current-workspace/requests/gap-analysis.json`), then: ```bash node apps/orchestrator-cli/src/main.mjs gap /path/to/gap-request.json ``` ## 6. Planning Use a change request JSON (see `examples/current-workspace/requests/`) and: ```bash node apps/orchestrator-cli/src/main.mjs plan /path/to/change-request.json ``` ## 7. Continuity (per repo workspace) From the **repository root** where you want `.foundry/` to live (often the monorepo root): ```bash cd /path/to/repo-root node /path/to/flagship-foundry-work/apps/orchestrator-cli/src/main.mjs init-project my-project "One-line objective" ``` This creates **`.foundry/projects/<name>/current-task.json`** and **`SDLC_CHARTER.md`** per **ADR-011**. ## 8. Control plane (optional) ```bash cd flagship-foundry-work npm run api ``` Configure auth per `README.md` (**ADR-006**). Use REST or the Cursor companion (`apps/cursor-companion/`). ## 9. Agents, skills, and pipeline Foundry does not install a separate “agent runtime.” Instead: - **Cursor / IDE**: `.cursor/rules`, `.cursor/skills`, `.cursor/agents` - **Claude Code**: `.claude/` as applicable - **Foundry continuity**: `.foundry/projects/<id>/` - **Codex legacy** (optional): `.codex/` may still exist for other tools - **CI gates**: `docs/ci-release-gates.md` (**ADR-009**) Align runbooks and personas from `runbooks/` and `personas/` with your process. ## 10. Verification ```bash cd flagship-foundry-work npm test npm run ci:targeted ``` ## References - [REPOSITORY_LAYOUT.md](../REPOSITORY_LAYOUT.md) - [adr-011-foundry-directory-layout-and-continuity-instance.md](../adr/adr-011-foundry-directory-layout-and-continuity-instance.md) - [docker-and-local-dev.md](../docker-and-local-dev.md)
