Each rule includes checklists for fool-proof AI-assisted development. **Version History:** - 2.1.0 - Web automation focus, removed irrelevant enterprise rules, added Playwright standards - 2.0.0 - Complete reorganization with SRP - 1.0.0 - Initial rules collection ==== RULE FILE: .cursor/rules/15-chome-extension/chrome-extension-master-standards-v2.md ==== # Chrome Extension Engineering Standard (CEES) Version: 2.0 (audit-based) Purpose: a single, comprehensive ruleset for building Manifest V3 Chrome extensions to a very high standard (security, privacy, maintainability, performance, and Chrome Web Store readiness). Designed to be pasted into a GPT workspace / interview environment. --- ## 0) Non‑negotiables ### Security & privacy - **Never ship secrets** in the extension package (API keys, usernames/passwords, private keys, tokens, test credentials, etc.). - **Never expose sensitive files via `web_accessible_resources`**. - **No PHI/PII in logs** (including debug logs) unless the user explicitly enables a “safe debug mode” that redacts by default. - **No remote code execution**: do not load or execute remote JavaScript/WASM. All executable code must ship with the extension. - **No `eval()` / `new Function()` / dynamic script strings**. ### Permissions - Default to **minimum permissions**. Every permission must map to a user-visible feature. - Prefer **optional permissions / optional host permissions** and request them **only at the moment a feature is enabled**. - If a feature is not enabled, the extension must still function without crashing. ### MV3 reality - The service worker **will be terminated frequently**. Everything must survive restarts. ### Chrome Web Store readiness - The extension must have a **single clear purpose**. - If user data is handled, an accurate **privacy policy** is required. - Do not collect browsing activity unless it is strictly required for the declared purpose. --- ## 1) Platform constraints you must design around ### 1.1 MV3 service worker lifecycle constraints - Treat the service worker as **ephemeral**: - No reliance on global state. - Persist all durable state. - Make every handler **idempotent**. - Every long-running workflow must be resumable. - Handlers must be structured as: 1) validate input + permissions 2) load state (storage) 3) perform bounded work 4) persist state 5) respond ### 1.2 Permission model constraints - Script injection (`chrome.scripting`) requires **host access** (either `activeTab` or host permissions). - Prefer a UX that requests host access **per site** and **only when needed**. - Assume host access can be denied; every feature must have a graceful failure path. ### 1.3 Web accessible resources constraints - `web_accessible_resources` is an allowlist of extension files that websites can fetch. - Treat it as a **public surface area**: if it’s web accessible, assume hostile sites can read it. ### 1.4 Storage constraints - Web Storage (`localStorage`) is not available in the service worker. - `chrome.storage.*` is JSON-based and quota-limited; use IndexedDB for larger data. --- ## 2) Architecture standard ### 2.1 Mandatory component boundaries - **UI surfaces** (side panel / popup / options) are “clients” and must not contain business logic. - **Service worker** is the orchestrator, but must be thin: - route messages - enforce permissions - enforce security policy - call domain services - **Domain services** (automation engine, storage, providers, telemetry) live in libraries and are unit-testable. - **Content scripts** are “adapters”: - minimal DOM work - no secrets - no persistent state ### 2.2 Message-driven, versioned protocol - All UI ↔ SW ↔ content-script interactions use a **single message protocol**. - Every message uses this envelope: - `type`: string literal union - `payload`: validated at runtime - `correlationId`: stable identifier for request/response pairs - `schemaVersion`: incremented when breaking changes occur - Reject unknown message types. ### 2.3 Trust boundaries & sender validation - Treat all inbound message payloads as untrusted. - For messages from content scripts, validate: - `sender.tab?.id` (expected tab) - `sender.url` (expected origin / match) - optional: handshake token established during injection ### 2.4 State & migrations - Every stored object has: - a schema (TypeScript type + runtime validation) - a `schemaVersion` - deterministic migrations - All migrations must be unit tested. ### 2.5 Configuration & feature flags - Remote configuration is allowed only as **data**, never as executable code. - Feature flags must be: - default-off for risky features - kill-switchable (disable without new release) --- ## 3) Security, privacy, and compliance ### 3.1 Data classification Classify every field as one of: - **Public**: safe anywhere. - **Internal**: safe in extension storage, not in logs. - **Sensitive**: credentials, tokens, personal identifiers. - **Regulated**: PHI/health, financial, government IDs. ### 3.2 Storage rules - **Credentials/tokens** - Prefer not storing. - If storing: encrypt-at-rest; keep in **session** by default; allow “remember me” only with explicit consent. - **Regulated data** - Default to session-only. - If persistence is required: user must opt-in; encryption, retention policy, and secure-delete workflow required. ### 3.3 Cryptography standard (WebCrypto) - Use `crypto.subtle` only (no custom crypto). - **AES-GCM** for encryption with: - random 96-bit IV per encryption - authentication enforced (no silent decrypt failures) - **KDF** for passphrase-derived keys: - PBKDF2 with a **random salt** stored alongside ciphertext - iteration count should be configurable and revisited periodically - **Never** use deterministic salts based on public data (like extension IDs). - Key management: - keys must be unlockable/rotatable - key material must not be written to disk unencrypted ### 3.4 Logging & telemetry - Logs must be structured. - Default logs include only: - event name - stable identifiers (non-sensitive) - timing - extension version - Sensitive/regulated content must be: - removed, or - replaced with stable hashes, or - redacted. ### 3.5 Network & exfiltration controls - All network access must be over HTTPS. - Maintain an allowlist of domains your extension contacts. - Never send sensitive/regulated data off-device without: - explicit user consent - documented retention - transport security ### 3.6 CSP rules - Keep CSP strict. - No `unsafe-eval`. - No inline scripts. ### 3.7 `web_accessible_resources` rules - Only include the minimum set of static assets required. - Never expose: - credential files - private keys - debug dumps - any file that can be used to fingerprint users or leak data - Restrict `matches` to only origins that need access. - Consider `use_dynamic_url` for resources that don’t need stable URLs. ### 3.8 External connectivity - `externally_connectable` is **off by default**. - If enabled, restrict to your owned domains and validate message origins. --- ## 4) API usage rules (high-impact) ### 4.1 `chrome.action` - If you define `action.default_popup`, do **not** rely on `chrome.action.onClicked`. - Treat `chrome.action.openPopup()` as best-effort (requires user gesture). ### 4.2 `chrome.permissions` - Use optional permissions/hosts and request at point-of-use. - Always show a human explanation in the UI before prompting. - Store per-feature permission state so you can explain why something is disabled. ### 4.3 `chrome.scripting` - Prefer declarative content scripts when possible. - If you must inject dynamically: - require user gesture - ensure host access exists - inject only bundled files (no code strings) - implement an “already injected?” handshake - avoid injecting repeatedly without idempotency guarantees ### 4.4 Messaging (`chrome.runtime.onMessage`, ports) - All message handlers must: - validate schema - validate sender - return structured errors - For async `sendResponse`, return `true` from the listener. - Prefer long-lived ports (`chrome.runtime.connect`) for streaming progress. ### 4.5 `chrome.storage` - Use the smallest appropriate store: - `session` for ephemeral - `local` for durable - `sync` only when explicitly needed - Do not store secrets unencrypted. - Implement write coalescing and avoid hot loops writing storage. ### 4.6 `chrome.alarms` - Use alarms only for coarse scheduling. - Always persist the job queue and recreate alarms on startup. - Never assume alarms persist across restarts. ### 4.7 Side panel - Side panel is the preferred “always-on” UI for complex flows. - Use it to host any long-lived UI state (e.g., unlocked session state). ### 4.8 `chrome.identity` - Prefer OAuth via `chrome.identity` for Google integrations. - Minimize scopes. - Never embed client secrets. ### 4.9 `chrome.cookies` - Requires explicit justification; only use if essential. - Keep host permissions narrow. ### 4.10 Network interception - Prefer `declarativeNetRequest` over `webRequest` where possible. --- ## 5) Implementation process (surgical iteration) ### 5.1 Feature slice template For each feature, produce these artifacts: 1. **One-sentence purpose** (user-visible). 2. **Permission delta**: changes in `permissions`, `host_permissions` / `optional_host_permissions`, `web_accessible_resources`. 3. **Data delta**: what data is collected/stored, retention, redaction. 4. **Threat model**: misuse cases + mitigations. 5. **Architecture delta**: modules touched, message types added. 6. **Test plan**: unit + integration + e2e. 7. **Rollback strategy**: how to disable feature without bricking. ### 5.2 Definition of Done - Feature works after service worker restart. - No new required permissions without a user-facing feature. - No secrets. - Tests added. - Logs are PHI-safe. --- ## 6) PR checklist - [ ] Manifest diff reviewed (permissions, hosts, `web_accessible_resources`). - [ ] Message schemas updated and validated. - [ ] Sender validation exists for new message paths. - [ ] Storage writes have schemas + migrations. - [ ] Long workflows checkpoint/resume. - [ ] No secrets added. - [ ] CSP unchanged or tightened. - [ ] E2E test updated or added. --- ## 7) Release and operational readiness ### 7.1 Build & reproducibility - Builds must be deterministic from lockfiles. - Bundle analysis must exist for size regressions. ### 7.2 Key management (stable IDs) - Never commit private keys. - If stable unpacked-extension IDs are required, use a **public key** (manifest `key`) derived from a PEM keypair, and store it safely. - Public keys may be committed if that aligns with your distribution model; private keys never. ### 7.3 Pre-submission checklist - Verify: - permissions are minimal - privacy policy is accurate - data handling disclosures match reality - no PHI/PII in logs - no remote code --- ## 8) Audit checklists ### 8.1 Security audit checklist - [ ] No secrets in repo or build output. - [ ] No secrets in `web_accessible_resources`. - [ ] Host permissions minimized; optional where possible. - [ ] Sender validation on all inbound messages. - [ ] Encryption-at-rest for sensitive data. ### 8.2 Performance audit checklist - [ ] No tight polling loops. - [ ] Storage writes coalesced. - [ ] Content scripts minimal and page-safe. ### 8.3 Reliability audit checklist - [ ] Works after SW restart. - [ ] Jobs resume from checkpoints. - [ ] Alarms recreated on startup. --- ## 9) GPT workspace “system prompt” (paste into your workspace) You are a staff-level Chrome extension engineer working in a monorepo. Rules: - Follow CEES strictly. - Before writing code, produce a plan with: permission delta, message schema delta, data delta, tests. - Implement minimal diffs. - Never introduce secrets. - If any change touches permissions or `web_accessible_resources`, explicitly justify it and propose a safer alternative. Commands: - `/spec` Produce the feature slice template. - `/design` Produce architecture + message schemas. - `/impl` Implement minimal diff in TypeScript. - `/test` Produce unit/integration/e2e test plan and code. - `/review` Run PR checklist against the diff. ==== RULE FILE: .cursor/rules/15-chome-extension/RULES_AUDIT.md ==== # Chrome Extension Rules Audit Report **Date**: 2025-01-15 **Scope**: All Chrome extension rules and project analysis **Projects Analyzed**: - `apps/chrome-extensions/PMHNP-Administration-SummerySky` - `apps/chrome-extensions/job-hunt-extension` ## Executive Summary This audit identified **5 major gaps** in Chrome extension rules covering batch operations, checkpoints/resume, error recovery, state persistence, and comprehensive logging. All gaps have been addressed with new comprehensive rule files. ## Rules Audited ### Existing Rules (15 files) 1. ✅ `build-and-serve.mdc` - Build commands and dist output 2. ✅ `chrome-extension-app-structure.mdc` - MV3 app structure 3. ✅ `chrome-extension-e2e-testing.mdc` - E2E testing standards 4. ✅ `code-style-and-structure.mdc` - TypeScript conventions 5. ✅ `flows-spec-and-execution.mdc` - Recipe spec and execution 6. ⚠️ `logging-and-observability.mdc` - **ENHANCED** (was minimal, now comprehensive) 7. ✅ `messaging-contracts.mdc` - MV3 messaging contracts 8. ✅ `mv3-lifecycle-and-state.mdc` - Service worker lifecycle 9. ✅ `playwright-and-e2e.mdc` - Playwright expectations 10. ✅ `prompts-and-workflows.mdc` - Workflow expectations 11. ✅ `repo-conventions.mdc` - Repository conventions 12. ✅ `security-and-permissions.mdc` - Security standards 13. ✅ `selectors-and-waits.mdc` - Selector resilience 14. ✅ `sidepanel-application-model.mdc` - Sidepanel state model 15. ✅ `summerysky-extension-standards.mdc` - SummerySky-specific standards ## Gaps Identified ### 1. Batch Operations ❌ → ✅ FIXED **Gap**: No rule covering batch execution patterns, concurrency control, pause/resume, deferred tasks, or state persistence for batch operations. **Evidence Found**: - `@chrome-ext/automation-batch` library extensively used in both projects - BatchRunner implementation with worker pools, retry logic, deferred tasks - Batch state persistence in `chrome.storage.local` - PHI-safe batch operations with secure storage **Impact**: High - Batch operations are critical for both projects but lacked standardized patterns. **Resolution**: Created `batch-operations.mdc` covering: - BatchRunner integration patterns - Task definition and ID requirements - Concurrency control guidelines - Service worker handlers - State persistence and resume - Error handling and retry policies - Deferred task handling - UI integration patterns - PHI-safe batch operations ### 2. Checkpoints and Resume ❌ → ✅ FIXED **Gap**: No rule covering checkpoint-based resumption for long-running recipe executions. **Evidence Found**: - Checkpoint system implemented in both projects - `saveCheckpoint` and `restoreCheckpoint` recipe step types - Checkpoint hooks for post-processing (e.g., converting checkpoints to postings) - UI integration for listing and resuming checkpoints - Checkpoint storage in `chrome.storage.local` **Impact**: High - Checkpoints are essential for long-running extractions but lacked documentation. **Resolution**: Created `checkpoints-and-resume.mdc` covering: - Checkpoint system overview - Storage structure and location - Recipe step types (saveCheckpoint, restoreCheckpoint) - Checkpoint implementation patterns - Checkpoint hooks - Naming conventions - UI integration - Error handling - Best practices ### 3. Error Recovery ❌ → ✅ FIXED **Gap**: No comprehensive rule covering graceful error handling, retry logic, circuit breakers, or error classification. **Evidence Found**: - Retry logic with exponential backoff in recipe executor - Circuit breaker pattern in batch operations - Transient vs permanent error classification - Error recovery strategies in both projects - Idempotent step execution patterns **Impact**: High - Error recovery is critical for reliable automation but lacked standardized patterns. **Resolution**: Created `error-recovery.mdc` covering: - Error classification (transient vs permanent) - Exponential backoff with jitter - Retry implementation patterns - Circuit breaker pattern - Idempotent operations - Error recovery strategies - Graceful degradation - Error logging ### 4. State Persistence ⚠️ → ✅ ENHANCED **Gap**: `mv3-lifecycle-and-state.mdc` covers basic state persistence but lacks details on: - Batch state persistence patterns - Checkpoint state management - State rehydration after suspension - State cleanup policies **Evidence Found**: - BatchStateStore for batch run persistence - Checkpoint storage patterns - State rehydration on service worker wake - Stale state cleanup logic **Impact**: Medium - Basic patterns exist but need enhancement. **Resolution**: Enhanced existing rule and added cross-references to new rules. ### 5. Logging and Observability ⚠️ → ✅ ENHANCED **Gap**: Original rule was minimal (13 lines). Missing: - Structured logging patterns - Batch operation logging - Checkpoint logging - Error logging with context - State transition logging - Performance logging - PHI-safe logging **Evidence Found**: - Comprehensive logging throughout codebase - Correlation ID usage - Run log storage in `chrome.storage.session` - Log export functionality - PHI-safe logging patterns **Impact**: High - Logging is critical for debugging but rule was too minimal. **Resolution**: Enhanced `logging-and-observability.mdc` from 13 lines to comprehensive guide covering: - Logger usage and levels - Structured logging with required context - Run log storage - Recipe execution logging - Batch operation logging - Checkpoint logging - Error logging - State transition logging - Sidepanel log display - Log export - PHI-safe logging - Performance logging ## New Rules Created ### 1. `batch-operations.mdc` (NEW) **Purpose**: Standardize batch operation patterns for concurrent recipe execution. **Key Sections**: - Architecture and BatchRunner integration - Task definition and ID requirements - Batch run options and concurrency guidelines - Service worker handlers - State persistence and resume - Error handling and retry policies - Deferred tasks - UI integration - PHI-safe batch operations - Logging patterns - Best practices and checklist ### 2. `checkpoints-and-resume.mdc` (NEW) **Purpose**: Standardize checkpoint-based resumption for long-running recipes. **Key Sections**: - Checkpoint system overview - Storage structure and location - Recipe step types - Implementation patterns - Checkpoint hooks - Naming conventions - UI integration - Error handling - Best practices and checklist ### 3. `error-recovery.mdc` (NEW) **Purpose**: Standardize error handling, retry logic, and recovery patterns. **Key Sections**: - Error classification (transient vs permanent) - Exponential backoff with jitter - Retry implementation - Circuit breaker pattern - Idempotent operations - Error recovery strategies - Graceful degradation - **Cross-Reference Updates**: Maintain consistency between related rules - **Version Bumps**: Update version numbers and change logs ### Edit Constraints - **NO Breaking Changes**: Never remove existing functionality without explicit approval - **Preserve Structure**: Maintain existing file organization and section hierarchy - **Update References**: Ensure all cross-references remain valid - **Test Compatibility**: Verify edits don't break existing rule relationships ## 🔧 Surgical Edit Protocol ### Step 1: Impact Assessment ```markdown Before making any edit: - [ ] Identify all files that reference the target content - [ ] Assess downstream effects on dependent rules - [ ] Check for version dependencies - [ ] Verify backward compatibility ``` ### Step 2: Atomic Changes ```markdown Each edit must be: - [ ] Self-contained (no external dependencies) - [ ] Reversible (can be undone without side effects) - [ ] Documented (clear change description) - [ ] Tested (verified against existing content) ``` ### Step 3: Validation Checks ```markdown After making changes: - [ ] Cross-reference integrity maintained - [ ] All linked examples still valid - [ ] Rule hierarchy preserved - [ ] No orphaned references created ``` ## 🎨 Edit Categories ### Configuration Edits ```markdown # ✅ ALLOWED: Update configuration values OLD: timeout: 10000 NEW: timeout: 15000 # ✅ ALLOWED: Add new configuration options OLD: timeout: 10000 NEW: timeout: 10000, retries: 3 # ❌ NOT ALLOWED: Remove configuration without replacement OLD: timeout: 10000, retries: 3 NEW: timeout: 10000 ``` ### Content Edits ```markdown # ✅ ALLOWED: Add clarifying information OLD: Use this method for API calls. Step one 2. Step two NEW: 1. Step one 2. Step two 3. Step three # ❌ NOT ALLOWED: Remove major sections OLD: ## Implementation ## Examples NEW: ## Implementation ``` ## 🔍 Validation Commands ### Pre-Edit Checks ```bash # Verify rule file integrity find .cursor/rules -name "*.mdc" -exec echo "Checking: {}" \; # Check for broken cross-references grep -r "\]\(" .cursor/rules/ | grep -v "http" | wc -l ``` ### Post-Edit Validation ```bash # Verify all files still parse correctly find .cursor/rules -name "*.mdc" -exec head -1 {} \; | grep -v "^#" # Check for orphaned references grep -r "](#" .cursor/rules/ | grep -v "\.mdc" | sort | uniq ``` ## 🚨 Emergency Rollback If a surgical edit causes issues: 1. **Immediate Revert**: Undo the change within 5 minutes 2. **Impact Assessment**: Document what broke and why 3. **Alternative Approach**: Implement fix using different method 4. **Prevention**: Add the problematic pattern to "NOT ALLOWED" list ## 📊 Success Metrics - **Zero Breaking Changes**: No edits that break existing functionality - **100% Reference Integrity**: All cross-references remain valid - **< 5 min Validation**: Each edit validates in under 5 minutes - **Clear Documentation**: Every edit has clear reasoning and impact ## 🔗 Related Rules - [chrome-extension-app-structure](../15-chome-extension/chrome-extension-app-structure.mdc) - For structural changes - [code-style-and-structure](../15-chome-extension/code-style-and-structure.mdc) - For code formatting consistency - [messaging-contracts](../15-chome-extension/messaging-contracts.mdc) - For communication protocol updates ## 📝 Change Log ### Version 1.0.0 - Initial surgical edits protocol established - Validation procedures defined - Edit categories documented - Emergency rollback process created ==== RULE FILE: .codex/README.md ==== # Codex Continuity Files This directory is the machine-readable continuity layer for Codex work in this workspace. ## Read Order 1. `.codex/projects/<project>/current-task.json` 2. `.codex/projects/<project>/SDLC_CHARTER.md` 3. **Recursive Search**: Finds all `.md` files in the specified folder and subfolders - **Duplicate Prevention**: Automatically deletes existing master files to prevent duplication - **Organized Output**: Creates `master-{folder-name}-documentation.md` in the target folder - **Structured Content**: Each file becomes a numbered section with file path reference - **Error Handling**: Continues processing even if individual files have errors ### Example ```bash # Generate master documentation for Chrome Extension API docs node generate-master-documentation.cjs chrome-ext-api # This creates: chrome-ext-api/master-chrome-ext-api-documentation.md ``` ### Output Structure The generated master file includes: - Header with generation timestamp and file count - Numbered sections for each `.md` file - File path references for each section - Original content from each file - Section separators between files ### Testing The script has been tested on the `chrome-ext-api` folder containing 70 `.md` files (1 root + 69 in subfolder), successfully generating a 30,000+ line master documentation file. ==== RULE FILE: docx-generation-export/README.md ==== # DOCX Generation Modules Standalone extraction of the DOCX generation modules and supporting components from the patient-record-generation app. Generates Microsoft Word (.docx) documents from encounter JSON records with configurable styles, headers, and page layout. ## Contents - **src/docx/** – Core DOCX generation - `docx-generator.ts` – Main generator (Document, sections, numbering, header) - `docx-styles.ts` – Style config (title, headings, body, field label/value, header table, page margins) - `docx-header.ts` – Header table (patient info, DOB, MRN, column widths, borders) - `index.ts` – Public API - **src/types/encounter-types.ts** – TypeScript types (EncounterRecord, Block, DocxStyleConfig, EncounterHeader, etc.) - **src/cli/generate-docx.ts** – CLI for single file, patient folder, or batch ## Install ```bash cd docx-generation-export npm install # or: pnpm install ``` ## Usage ### Programmatic ```ts import { generateDocx, createDocxGenerator, DEFAULT_DOCX_STYLE_CONFIG } from './src/docx/index.js'; import type { EncounterRecord } from './src/types/encounter-types.js'; const encounter: EncounterRecord = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('encounter.json', 'utf-8')); const buffer = await generateDocx(encounter, { includeHeader: true }); fs.writeFileSync('output.docx', buffer); ``` ### CLI ```bash # Single file npx tsx src/cli/generate-docx.ts --input=path/to/encounter.json # Custom output npx tsx src/cli/generate-docx.ts --input=encounter.json --output=out.docx # All JSONs in a patient folder (expects patient folder to have encounters/ subdir) npx tsx src/cli/generate-docx.ts --patient=patient-12345 # All patient folders (default base: output/Bravado-Unified-Patient-Folders) npx tsx src/cli/generate-docx.ts --all # Help npx tsx src/cli/generate-docx.ts --help ``` ## Encounter JSON shape Input JSON must be an `IDEEncounterRecord` or `MMEEncounterRecord`: `schemaVersion`, `encounter`, `patient`, `provider`, `clinical`, `header` (with `table.rows`), and `blocks` (title, heading, paragraph, bullets). See `src/types/encounter-types.ts` for full definitions. ## Dependencies - **docx** (^8.6.0) – Word document generation - **tsx** (dev) – Run TypeScript CLI - **typescript** (dev) – Build ## License Same as the source workspace. ==== RULE FILE: libs/cursor-flow/README.md ==== # Cursor Flow - Web Automation Made Easy A comprehensive web automation system for creating, editing, and managing automated workflows with AI assistance. ## 🚀 Features - **🎯 Visual Flow Editor**: Create and edit automation flows with a user-friendly interface - **🤖 AI-Powered**: Generate flows automatically using AI models - **📦 Staging & Promotion**: Test flows in staging before promoting to production - **🔧 Step Management**: Add, edit, move, and delete individual steps - **🎨 Element Picker**: Visually select elements on web pages - **📊 Observability**: Comprehensive logging and action tracking - **🔄 Bridge Communication**: Seamless integration with backend platforms ## 📋 Architecture The cursor-flow system consists of several key components: ### Core Components 1. **FlowEditorUI** (`src/ui/FlowEditorUI.ts`) - Main UI component for flow editing - Handles modal display and user interactions - Manages flow state and step editing 2. **FlowEditor** (`src/ui/flow/FlowEditor.ts`) - Core business logic for flow management - Implements the `FlowEditorApi` interface - Handles flow validation and step operations 3. **CursorCLIIntegration** (`src/cursorCLI.ts`) - Interface for AI model integration - Handles flow generation and optimization 4. **StagingWorkflowManager** (`src/stagingWorkflow.ts`) - Manages flow deployment lifecycle - Handles staging, testing, and promotion ### Interface Definition The `FlowEditorApi` interface defines the contract for flow editing operations: ```typescript interface FlowEditorApi { getSteps(): FlowStepDef[] setSteps(steps: FlowStepDef[]): void append(step: FlowStepDef): void loadFlow(flow: Flow): void getFlow(): Flow addStep(step: FlowStep): void moveStep(fromIndex: number, toIndex: number): void validateFlow(): void updateStepLocator(stepIndex: number, locator: any): void saveFlow(): void canRunFlow(): boolean updateContent(content: string): void } ``` ## 🎯 Usage ### Basic Flow Creation 1. **Open Editor**: Click the "Open Editor" button in the main menu 2. **Create Flow**: Click "Create New Flow" to start a new automation 3. **Add Steps**: Use the step editor to add individual actions 4. **Configure Elements**: Use the element picker to select page elements 5. **Save & Test**: Save your flow and test it in the staging environment 6. **Promote**: Move successful flows to production ### Step Types The system supports various step types: - **click**: Click on an element - **type**: Type text into an input field - **select**: Select an option from a dropdown - **goto**: Navigate to a URL - **waitFor**: Wait for an element or condition - **assertVisible**: Assert that an element is visible - **assertText**: Assert that text is present - **iterate**: Repeat steps for multiple elements ### Element Locators Elements can be located using various strategies: - **CSS Selectors**: `.button`, `#element-id` - **Text Content**: Elements containing specific text - **ARIA Roles**: `button`, `textbox`, etc. - **Labels**: Form elements with specific labels - **Placeholders**: Input fields with placeholder text - **Test IDs**: Elements with `data-testid` attributes ## 🔧 Bridge Events The system uses bridge events for communication between the overlay and platform: ### Outgoing Events (from overlay to platform) - `openEditor`: Open the flow editor modal - `saveSteps`: Save flow steps to storage - `runDraft`: Execute the current draft flow - `promoteDraft`: Promote draft to production - `testFlow`: Test flow in staging environment - `generateFlow`: Generate flow using AI ### Incoming Events (from platform to overlay) - `cursorflow:testResults`: Test execution results - `cursorflow:aiSuggestions`: AI-generated step suggestions ## 🧪 Testing ### Running Tests ```bash # Run all tests npm test # Run specific test files npm test FlowEditorUI.spec.ts # Run tests with coverage npm test -- --coverage ``` ### Test Structure - **Unit Tests**: Test individual components in isolation - **Integration Tests**: Test component interactions - **E2E Tests**: Test complete user workflows ## 📊 Observability The system provides comprehensive observability features: ### Action Tracking Every action is tracked with timing information: ``` 🔄 Action started: openEditor at 2025-09-24T00:18:26.727Z ✅ Action completed: openEditor in 150ms ``` ### Bridge Communication Logging All bridge events are logged for debugging: ``` [CursorFlow] 🔓 User clicked Open Editor button [CursorFlow] Bridge function found, calling... 🎯 Handling bridge event: openEditor 🎯 Opening Cursor Flow Editor via bridge event ``` ### Error Handling Errors are caught and logged with context: ``` ❌ Action failed: generateFlow after 3000ms Error: AI service unavailable ``` ## 🚀 Development ### Setting Up Development Environment 1. **Install Dependencies** ```bash npm install ``` 2. **Start Development Server** ```bash npm run dev ``` 3. **Run Tests** ```bash npm test ``` ### Building for Production ```bash npm run build ``` ### Code Quality - **Modular architecture** - Pick and choose only the modules you need - **Pluggable authentication** - Support for Google, Microsoft, Social, SSO, and Email/password - **MV3 compliant** - Service worker, promises, and modern Chrome APIs - **Fluid design system** - Responsive typography and spacing using `clamp()` and viewport units - **Side panel support** - Optional MV3 side panel UI (Chrome 114+) - **Type-safe** - Full TypeScript support with strict typing - **Observable** - Structured logging, correlation IDs, and metrics ## Library Structure ``` libs/Google-Chrome-Extension-Library/ ├── core/ │ ├── runtime/ # MV3 scaffolding, manifest builder, message bus │ ├── storage/ # chrome.storage wrappers with namespacing │ └── telemetry/ # Structured logging, correlation IDs, metrics ├── ui/ │ └── design-tokens/ # Fluid typography/spacing tokens └── auth/ ├── base/ # AuthProvider interface and registry ├── google/ # Google Identity API provider ├── microsoft/ # Azure AD provider ├── social/ # OAuth2 social providers ├── sso/ # OIDC/SAML providers └── email/ # Email/password provider ``` ## Quick Start ### Installation Import the modules you need: ```typescript import { buildManifest, bootstrapBackground } from '@chrome-ext/core-runtime'; import { ChromeStorage } from '@chrome-ext/core-storage'; import { logger } from '@chrome-ext/core-telemetry'; import { googleProvider } from '@chrome-ext/auth-google'; import { microsoftProvider } from '@chrome-ext/auth-microsoft'; import { registerProviders } from '@chrome-ext/auth-base'; ``` ### Basic Usage #### 1. Build Manifest ```typescript import { buildManifest } from '@chrome-ext/core-runtime'; const manifest = buildManifest({ name: 'My Extension', version: '1.0.0', permissions: ['storage', 'identity'], sidePanel: { defaultPath: 'sidepanel.html', }, oauth2: { clientId: 'your-google-client-id', scopes: ['openid', 'profile', 'email'], }, }); ``` #### 2. Setup Background Service Worker ```typescript import { bootstrapBackground, setupSidePanel } from '@chrome-ext/core-runtime'; bootstrapBackground({ onInstalled: async (details) => { console.log('Extension installed:', details.reason); await setupSidePanel({ openPanelOnActionClick: true, defaultPath: 'sidepanel.html', }); }, }); ``` #### 3. Setup Authentication ```typescript import { registerProviders } from '@chrome-ext/auth-base'; import { googleProvider } from '@chrome-ext/auth-google'; import { microsoftProvider } from '@chrome-ext/auth-microsoft'; const providers = registerProviders( googleProvider({ clientId: 'your-google-client-id', scopes: ['openid', 'profile', 'email'], }), microsoftProvider({ clientId: 'your-microsoft-client-id', scopes: ['openid', 'profile', 'email', 'User.Read'], }), ); // Use providers const googleAuth = providers.find(p => p.id === 'google'); if (googleAuth) { const result = await googleAuth.signIn(); console.log('Signed in:', result.user); } ``` #### 4. Use Storage ```typescript import { ChromeStorage } from '@chrome-ext/core-storage'; const storage = new ChromeStorage('local', 'my-namespace'); await storage.set('key', { value: 'data' }); const value = await storage.get('key'); ``` #### 5. Use Logging ```typescript import { logger } from '@chrome-ext/core-telemetry'; logger.info('User signed in', { userId: '123' }); logger.error('Sign-in failed', error, { provider: 'google' }); ``` ## Design Tokens Import the CSS file to use fluid design tokens: ```html <link rel="stylesheet" href="path/to/tokens.css"> ``` Tokens include: - **Fluid typography** using `clamp()` (H1, H2, H3, body, subtext, caption) - **Fluid spacing** (8-pt system with clamped values) - **Safe-area support** for mobile devices - **Container query units** for resizable panes - **Touch targets** (minimum 44×44px) ## Authentication Providers ### Google Uses MV3 Identity API (`chrome.identity.getAuthToken`): ```typescript import { googleProvider } from '@chrome-ext/auth-google'; const provider = googleProvider({ clientId: 'your-client-id', scopes: ['openid', 'profile', 'email'], }); const result = await provider().signIn(); ``` **Required manifest:** ```json { "oauth2": { "client_id": "your-client-id", "scopes": ["openid", "profile", "email"] }, "permissions": ["identity"] } ``` ### Microsoft Uses `chrome.identity.launchWebAuthFlow` with PKCE: ```typescript import { microsoftProvider } from '@chrome-ext/auth-microsoft'; const provider = microsoftProvider({ clientId: 'your-client-id', tenant: 'common', // or your tenant ID scopes: ['openid', 'profile', 'email', 'User.Read'], }); const result = await provider().signIn(); ``` ## Module Boundaries Libraries follow Nx module boundaries: - `core/*` - Runtime utilities (can be used by all) - `ui/*` - UI components and tokens (can be used by features) - `auth/*` - Authentication providers (can be used by features) ## Testing Each library includes test configuration: ```bash nx test chrome-ext-core-runtime nx test chrome-ext-auth-google ``` ## Contributing When adding new providers or modules: 1. Follow the existing structure 2. Implement the `AuthProvider` interface for auth providers 3. Export through `src/index.ts` 4. Add proper TypeScript types 5. To use it: ```bash # Build the library pnpm nx build web-documentation # Run the CLI pnpm nx run web-documentation:scrape -- <urls...> ``` ## Usage ### CLI Usage ```bash # Basic usage pnpm nx run web-documentation:scrape -- https://docs.example.com/api # Multiple URLs with custom output directory pnpm nx run web-documentation:scrape -- \ https://docs.example.com/api \ https://docs.example.com/guide \ --output-dir ./documentation # With numbered filenames pnpm nx run web-documentation:scrape -- \ https://docs.example.com/api \ --output-dir ./docs \ --numbered # Use browser automation for dynamic API documentation pnpm nx run web-documentation:scrape -- \ https://api.example.com/docs \ --browser \ --headed \ --output-dir ./api-docs ``` ### Programmatic Usage ```typescript import { DocumentationScraper, MarkdownConverter, FileWriter } from '@mm/web-documentation'; // Initialize components const scraper = new DocumentationScraper({ userAgent: 'My-Scraper/1.0.0', timeout: 30000, }); const converter = new MarkdownConverter({ includeCodeExamples: true, includeApiReference: true, includeToc: true, }); const writer = new FileWriter(); // Scrape, convert, and save const urls = [ 'https://docs.zoominfo.com/reference/overview', 'https://docs.zoominfo.com/reference/searchinterface_searchcontact', ]; const pages = await scraper.scrapePages(urls); const docs = pages.map(page => converter.convert(page)); await writer.writeFiles(docs, './documentation-3rd-party/Zoom-Info-API'); ``` ## API Reference ### DocumentationScraper ```typescript class DocumentationScraper { constructor(options?: ScraperOptions); scrapePage(url: string): Promise<DocumentationPage>; scrapePages(urls: string[]): Promise<DocumentationPage[]>; } ``` ### MarkdownConverter ```typescript class MarkdownConverter { constructor(options?: ConverterOptions); convert(page: DocumentationPage): ScrapedDocumentation; } ``` ### FileWriter ```typescript class FileWriter { writeFile(doc: ScrapedDocumentation, outputPath: string): Promise<void>; writeFiles(docs: ScrapedDocumentation[], outputDir: string, filenamePattern?: Function): Promise<void>; } ``` ## Configuration Options ### ScraperOptions - `userAgent?: string` - Custom user agent string - `timeout?: number` - Request timeout in milliseconds (default: 30000) - `maxRetries?: number` - Maximum retry attempts (default: 3) - `retryDelay?: number` - Base delay between retries in milliseconds (default: 1000) - `useBrowser?: boolean` - Use browser automation for dynamic content (default: false) - `browserWaitTime?: number` - Wait time for dynamic content in milliseconds (default: 5000) - `headless?: boolean` - Run browser in headless mode (default: true) ### ConverterOptions - `includeCodeExamples?: boolean` - Include code blocks in output (default: true) - `includeApiReference?: boolean` - Include API reference sections (default: true) - `includeToc?: boolean` - Generate table of contents (default: true) - `frontmatter?: object` - Additional frontmatter metadata ## Output Format Each scraped page is converted to Markdown with frontmatter: ```markdown --- title: "Contacts" url: "https://docs.zoominfo.com/reference/searchinterface_searchcontact" scrapedAt: "2025-12-19T10:00:00.000Z" lastModified: "2025-12-19T09:00:00.000Z" --- # Contacts ## Overview This endpoint allows you to search for contacts... ``` ## ZoomInfo API Documentation This library was specifically designed to scrape ZoomInfo API documentation. The following URLs are commonly scraped: - `https://docs.zoominfo.com/reference/overview` - API Overview - `https://docs.zoominfo.com/reference/searchinterface_searchcontact` - Contacts Search - `https://docs.zoominfo.com/reference/enrichinterface_enrichcontact` - Contacts Enrichment - `https://docs.zoominfo.com/reference/lookupinterface_lookup` - Data Lookup - `https://docs.zoominfo.com/reference/userinterface_userusage` - Usage Data ### Example Command ```bash pnpm nx run web-documentation:scrape -- \ https://docs.zoominfo.com/reference/overview \ https://docs.zoominfo.com/reference/searchinterface_searchcontact \ https://docs.zoominfo.com/reference/enrichinterface_enrichcontact \ https://docs.zoominfo.com/reference/lookupinterface_lookup \ https://docs.zoominfo.com/reference/userinterface_userusage \ --output-dir documentation-3rd-party/Zoom-Info-API \ --numbered ``` This will create files like: - `001-overview.md` - `002-searchinterface_searchcontact.md` - `003-enrichinterface_enrichcontact.md` - `004-lookupinterface_lookup.md` - `005-userinterface_userusage.md` ## Dependencies - `jsdom` - HTML parsing and DOM manipulation - `tsx` - TypeScript execution for CLI ## Development ```bash # Build pnpm nx build web-documentation # Test pnpm nx test web-documentation # Lint pnpm nx lint web-documentation # Type check pnpm nx typecheck web-documentation ``` ## Error Handling The scraper includes robust error handling: - **Network failures**: Automatic retries with exponential backoff - **Invalid HTML**: Graceful fallback to basic text extraction - **Missing content**: Clear error messages for debugging - **Rate limiting**: Respects delays between requests ## Contributing 1. Go to [https://script.google.com/](https://script.google.com/) 2. Click **"New Project"** 3. Name your project (e.g., "IDE JSON to Docs Converter") ### Step 2: Copy the Script 1. Open `ide-json-to-docs.gs` from this repository 2. Copy the entire contents 3. Paste into the Google Apps Script editor (replacing any default code) ### Step 3: Configure the Script Update the `CONFIG` object at the top of the script: ```javascript const CONFIG = { // Root folder ID where ACTIVE/INACTIVE folders live rootFolderId: '1Tb5v39DqRwk2341iYwOKqMXxA3e1Iu-8', // Leave empty for auto-detection (recommended) statusFolder: '', patientName: '', // Paste your JSON here, or use jsonFileId jsonInput: '', jsonFileId: '', // Options createJsonCopy: true, includeMissingData: false, includeClinicalInferences: false, autoDetect: true, // Recommended: automatically detect patient name and status }; ``` ### Step 4: Grant Permissions 1. Click **"Run"** → **"generateRecordFromJson"** 2. When prompted, click **"Review Permissions"** 3. Select your Google account 4. Click **"Advanced"** → **"Go to [Project Name] (unsafe)"** 5. Click **"Allow"** to grant permissions: - Access to Google Drive (to create folders and files) - Access to Google Docs (to create documents) ## Usage ### Method 1: Paste JSON Directly (Recommended) 1. Copy the AI-generated JSON from your AI tool 2. In the script editor, paste it into `CONFIG.jsonInput`: ```javascript jsonInput: `{ "schemaVersion": "1.0", "encounterId": "ide-1766464684536-2022-09-01", ... }`, ``` 3. Ensure `autoDetect: true` in CONFIG 4. Click **"Run"** → **"generateRecordFromJson"** 5. The script will: - Automatically detect patient name from JSON header - Detect status (ACTIVE/INACTIVE) - Create/use the appropriate folder structure - Generate the Google Doc - Save a JSON copy in the patient folder ### Method 2: Use Drive File ID 1. Upload the JSON file to Google Drive 2. Get the file ID from the file URL: `https://drive.google.com/file/d/{FILE_ID}/view` 3. Set `CONFIG.jsonFileId` to the file ID: ```javascript jsonFileId: '1a2b3c4d5e6f7g8h9i0j', ``` 4. Click **"Run"** → **"generateRecordFromJson"** ## Folder Structure The script creates the following structure in Google Drive: ``` Root Folder (1Tb5v39DqRwk2341iYwOKqMXxA3e1Iu-8) ├── ACTIVE/ │ └── {Patient Name} - {patientId}/ │ ├── IDE - {date} - {Patient Name}.doc │ └── EncounterNoteDraft-IDE-{date}.json └── INACTIVE/ └── {Patient Name} - {patientId}/ └── ... ``` ## Auto-Detection Features When `autoDetect: true`: - **Patient Name**: Extracted from `draft.header.patientLegalName`, or searched for in existing folders by patient ID - **Status**: Detected from `draft.status` field, or defaults to "ACTIVE" for IDE notes - **Folder Matching**: If patient ID is found in encounterId (pattern: `ide-{patientId}-{date}`), searches existing folders to find the correct patient name ## Error Handling The script validates: - JSON syntax - Required fields: `schemaVersion`, `encounterId`, `noteType`, `dateOfService`, `sections`, `missingData`, `clinicalInferences` - Folder access permissions Common errors: - **"Invalid JSON"**: Check JSON syntax - **"Missing required field"**: Ensure all required fields are present - **"Cannot find folder"**: Verify `rootFolderId` is correct and you have access ## Configuration Options | Option | Description | Default | |--------|-------------|---------| | `rootFolderId` | Google Drive folder ID for patient records | Required | | `statusFolder` | "ACTIVE" or "INACTIVE" (empty for auto-detect) | '' | | `patientName` | Patient name (empty for auto-detect) | '' | | `jsonInput` | JSON string to paste directly | '' | | `jsonFileId` | Google Drive file ID containing JSON | '' | | `createJsonCopy` | Save JSON copy in patient folder | `true` | | `includeMissingData` | Include missingData section in doc | `false` | | `includeClinicalInferences` | Include clinicalInferences section | `false` | | `autoDetect` | Auto-detect patient name and status | `true` | ## Troubleshooting ### Script can't find root folder - Verify the folder ID is correct - Ensure you have access to the folder - Check that the folder exists ### Patient name not detected - Ensure `draft.header.patientLegalName` exists in JSON - Or manually set `CONFIG.patientName` - Check that patient ID pattern matches: `ide-{patientId}-{date}` ### Document not created - Check Google Apps Script execution log for errors - Verify all required permissions are granted - Ensure JSON structure matches EncounterNoteDraft schema ## Example JSON Structure The script expects JSON matching the EncounterNoteDraft schema: ```json { "schemaVersion": "1.0", "encounterId": "ide-1766464684536-2022-09-01", "noteType": "IDE", "dateOfService": "2022-09-01", "provider": "Dr. Smith", "header": { "patientLegalName": "DOE, JOHN", "dob": "1980-01-01", "mrn": "12345" }, "sections": [ { "title": "CHIEF COMPLAINT", "blocks": [ { "type": "paragraph", "text": "Patient presents with..." } ] } ], "missingData": [], "clinicalInferences": [] } ``` ## Support For issues or questions: 1. Check the execution log in Google Apps Script editor 2. Verify JSON structure matches the schema 3. Ensure all permissions are granted 4.
